distractorRationale.2: This sentence is about a single station's limited view of the wider pattern, not about any equipment problem at Halyard Point.
distractorRationale.3: The report calls the steady climb the one pattern underneath every local mystery this year has produced, which explicitly includes Halyard Point's, not just Sable Flats'.

items.explain: The synthesis draws the connection directly: a warmer average is why Halyard Point's spring keeps arriving earlier than the colony's food supply can follow, tying its local mystery to the same network-wide pattern explaining Sable Flats' dry years.  Each wrong choice tries to separate Halyard Point's mystery from that shared cause.

items.stem: Choose the three facts that together explain the colony's adaptation limit.
choices: The colony no longer lays any eggs before April.
The colony's first-egg date has moved twenty-eight days earlier over thirty seasons.
The herring's arrival date has held close to the same date every season.
The fledge rate has climbed as the nesting date moved earlier.
The herring's arrival date has also moved twenty-eight days earlier, matching the terns.
The colony's chicks now hatch weeks before the herring arrive.

distractorRationale.0: The thirtieth season's first eggs came on March tenth, before April even began, so the colony has not stopped laying eggs earlier than April.
distractorRationale.3: The fledge rate dropped from seventy-six percent in the first season to thirty-nine percent in the thirtieth, the opposite of climbing.
distractorRationale.4: The herring's arrival date has drifted by only about three days in either direction, nowhere close to the twenty-eight-day shift in the nesting date.

items.explain: The three correct facts trace the colony's actual adaptation limit: its nesting date shifted twenty-eight days earlier while the herring's own arrival date barely moved, so the chicks now hatch weeks before their food source arrives, which is exactly the mismatch the record's fledge-rate column tracks.  The three wrong choices each invert a number the record reports in the opposite direction.

items.stem: Tap the two sentences that state what the fledge-rate column has actually been tracking all along.
spans: The gap between the two dates is what the fledge-rate column has been tracking.
It was never the nesting date by itself.
The colony is not nesting earlier by chance, since terns time their first eggs to the spring air and water.
The colony's chicks now hatch weeks before their food source even arrives.
items.explain: Both correct sentences state the record's own conclusion directly: the fledge-rate column tracks the growing gap between the two dates, not the nesting date on its own.  The other two sentences explain why the nesting date shifted and describe the consequence for the chicks, real details, but neither one is the record's own naming of what the column tracks.

items.stem: Tap the two sentences that describe a signal bouncing up and down rather than climbing steadily.
spans: Some years rose sharply.
One year barely rose at all.
Not one of the past ten years has dropped back.
That climb has stayed steady, year after year.
items.explain: Both correct sentences describe the temperature line's up-and-down bounce, some years rising sharply and other years barely rising at all, the pattern the report ties to short-term natural causes.  The other two sentences describe the carbon dioxide and fuel-use lines instead, which never drop back and climb by a steady amount every year.

items.stem: That {{0}} runs slower than the coastal air the terns respond to.

choices: clock
gap
mark

distractorRationale.1: The gap is the growing difference between the nesting date and the herring's arrival date, not the herring's own internal timing mechanism.
distractorRationale.2: The warm mark is the temperature threshold the terns respond to, a different animal's cue, not the herring's own ocean-temperature timing.

items.quote: That clock runs slower than the coastal air the terns respond to.
items.explain: The record names the herring's own ocean-temperature timing mechanism a clock, and states it runs slower than the coastal air signal the terns respond to, which is exactly why the two species' schedules have drifted apart.  Gap and mark each name a different piece of the record's own vocabulary, not the herring's timing mechanism itself.

items.stem: Over the thirty logged seasons, how did the herring's arrival date compare to the tern colony's nesting date?
choices: The herring's arrival date barely moved while the nesting date shifted twenty-eight days earlier.
Both dates shifted by almost exactly the same amount, staying in step with each other.
The herring's arrival date shifted earlier by even more than the nesting date did.
Neither date changed at all across the thirty seasons.

distractorRationale.1: The record reports a twenty-eight-day shift in the nesting date against only about a three-day drift in the herring's arrival date, far from matching each other.
distractorRationale.2: The record states the herring's arrival date has held near April twenty-first every season, drifting only about three days, nowhere close to the nesting date's twenty-eight-day shift.
distractorRationale.3: The nesting date moved from April seventh in the first season to March tenth in the thirtieth, a real and recorded twenty-eight-day change.

items.explain: The thirty-season record shows two very different clocks: the tern colony's first-egg date moved twenty-eight days earlier over thirty seasons, responding to warming coastal air, while the herring's own ocean-temperature-driven arrival date held close to the same date, drifting only about three days either way, which is why the colony's chicks now hatch weeks before the herring arrive.

items.stem: A new instrument at a different station logs a number that rises sharply one year, drops the next, then rises again the year after.  Based on the synthesis report's own reasoning, what does this pattern most likely point to?
choices: A steady, human-linked cause, since any change at all over three years counts as the same kind of signal.
A short-term natural cause, since the number is bouncing up and down rather than climbing steadily.
An instrument malfunction, since real data should never rise and fall from year to year.
Nothing can be concluded from only three years of a new instrument's data.

distractorRationale.0: The report specifically distinguishes a bouncing signal from a steady one; a number that rises, drops, then rises again is bouncing, not climbing the same amount every year the way carbon dioxide and fuel use do.
distractorRationale.2: The report treats the temperature line's own up-and-down bounce as normal and expected, caused by ordinary short-term factors, not as evidence of broken equipment.
distractorRationale.3: The report does draw a conclusion from a bouncing pattern like this one: it treats that up-and-down shape itself as the signature of short-term natural causes, distinct from a steady climbing trend.

items.explain: Network Command's own rule distinguishes the two shapes directly: a signal that bounces up and down, some years rising sharply and other years barely moving, points to short-term natural causes, while only a signal that climbs by close to the same steady amount every year, without ever reversing, points to the network's ongoing, human-linked pattern.  A rise-drop-rise instrument reading matches the bouncing shape, not the steady one.

items.stem: According to the synthesis report, why can a single field station not see the network's full warming pattern on its own?
choices: A single station's instruments are never accurate enough to be trusted.
Network Command deliberately hides the combined data from individual stations.
A lone station can only see its own local report, not the pattern across every station and year together.
Each station's local mystery has nothing to do with any of the others.

distractorRationale.0: The report never questions any single station's instrument accuracy.  Its point is about scope, one report versus every station's reports together, not about accuracy.
distractorRationale.1: The report never describes Command withholding data.  It explains that the pattern only becomes visible once every station's separate reports are read side by side.
distractorRationale.3: The report's entire point is the opposite: every local mystery, Halyard Point's and Sable Flats', turns out to share the same underlying planetary cause once read together.

items.explain: The synthesis report states plainly that one station cannot see a planetary pattern and cannot see past its own single report, which is exactly why the pattern only becomes visible once the network reads every station's local mystery side by side, rather than any one relay's readings being unreliable or hidden.

items.stem: In eight words or fewer, name what the record shows chicks now do relative to their food source, the real cause behind the falling fledge rate.
accept: they hatch before the herring arrives
the chicks hatch before the herring
hatch before their food source arrives
hatch before the herring shows up
items.explain: The record's own closing description names the real cause directly: the colony's chicks now hatch weeks before the herring, their one food source, even arrive, a reversal from the colony's early seasons, when the herring were already there and settled in.  It was never simply the nesting date by itself that mattered.

partA.stem: Which proposal fails Command's constraint that the response must use only authority the Network already holds?
choices: Proposal C, since it depends on a fishery authority that does not answer to the Network.
Proposal A, since the Network has never run a feeding station before.
Proposal B, since fencing requires authority the Network does not have over its own land.
All three proposals fail this constraint equally.

partB.stem: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer you just gave?
choices: That authority covers its posts and the land around them.
The Network runs feeding stations at two other posts.
The fishery authority does not answer to the Network, though.
The authority to run one is not in question.

distractorRationale.1: This sentence says the Network already runs feeding stations at two other posts, which means it has done this before, not never.
distractorRationale.2: This sentence says the Network's own authority covers its posts and the land around them, exactly where fencing would go, so fencing does not require authority it lacks.
distractorRationale.3: This sentence says the authority question for Proposal A is not even in question, meaning it clearly passes, so the three proposals do not all fail equally.

items.explain: The report states plainly that the fishery authority does not answer to the Network, which means Proposal C would need cooperation from outside the Network's own authority, exactly the kind of authority Command's third constraint rules out.  The other choices each misread which proposal actually has that authority problem.

partA.stem: Proposal B fits Command's time and cost limits easily.  Why might it still fail to solve the colony's actual problem?
choices: The record shows chicks are starving during the food gap, a problem fencing against predators does not touch.
The fencing would cost far more than the field budget allows.
Fencing cannot be built within the one-season time limit Command set.
The Network lacks the authority to build fencing on its own land.

partB.stem: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer you just gave?
choices: That authority covers its posts and the land around them.
It can go up within days.
Fencing does nothing to touch that problem.
The fencing is inexpensive.

distractorRationale.1: This sentence says the fencing is inexpensive, the opposite of costing far more than the budget allows.
distractorRationale.2: This sentence says fencing can go up within days, well within any one-season time limit.
distractorRationale.3: This sentence says the Network's own authority covers its posts and the land around them, exactly where fencing would go.

items.explain: The report names the real weakness directly: the record shows chicks starving during the gap before the herring arrive, and fencing, which only keeps predators away from eggs and chicks, does nothing to touch that specific problem, even though it easily satisfies every one of Command's other constraints.  Each wrong choice invents a time, cost, or authority problem the report explicitly rules out.

partA.stem: An operative back at Sable Flats logs one unusually wet week and radios that the post's climate has changed.  What is the flaw in that call?
choices: One week of weather is not the same as a change in the long-term climate pattern averaged over years.
Sable Flats never receives rain of any kind, so the report must be a mistake.
Climate and weather mean exactly the same thing, so the call is correct.
The operative should have checked whether the wind belt shifted before saying anything.

partB.stem: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer you just gave?
choices: Weather is what is happening outside the window this morning.
A single storm or a single clear week can happen at either station.
Climate is the pattern averaged over years.
These long-term patterns do not change because of one storm.

distractorRationale.1: This sentence says the opposite: long-term patterns do not change because of one storm, so a single storm cannot prove the climate itself has changed.
distractorRationale.2: This sentence defines weather narrowly, as what is happening outside the window this morning, a single moment, which the passage treats as different from climate, the pattern averaged over years.
distractorRationale.3: This sentence is about a single storm or clear week happening at a station, not about checking wind belts specifically, which the passage never suggests as a required step here.

items.explain: The passage draws the distinction directly: climate is the pattern averaged over years, while a single storm or a single clear week, exactly like the wet week the operative logged, can happen at either station without its long-term climate actually changing.  Each wrong choice either denies that distinction or invents a step the passage never asks for.

partA.stem: A new operative argues that this year's especially warm reading at one station is, by itself, solid proof of the network's warming pattern.  What is the flaw in that argument?
choices: A single year's temperature reading bounces naturally, so only the longer, steady trend across many stations and years actually counts as evidence.
Temperature readings are never reliable at any single station.
The warming pattern can only be proven using carbon dioxide data, never temperature.
One especially warm year always matches the carbon dioxide trend exactly.

partB.stem: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer you just gave?
choices: Every station on the network logs its local temperature.
Every station's air-sampling equipment also logs atmospheric carbon dioxide.
A signal that bounces up and down, like the temperature line, usually points to short-term natural causes.
Some years rose sharply.

distractorRationale.1: This sentence says every station logs its own local temperature as a matter of course, which the network clearly treats as usable data, not something unreliable.
distractorRationale.2: This sentence says carbon dioxide is another number the network tracks, alongside temperature, not the only signal that can count as evidence.
distractorRationale.3: This sentence says some years rose sharply while others barely rose at all, which is exactly the bounce that does not match carbon dioxide's steady, unbroken climb.

items.explain: The synthesis explains why a single warm year is not solid proof: a signal that bounces up and down, like the temperature line, usually points to short-term natural causes, and only a steady climb across many years and every station, the way carbon dioxide and fuel use behave together, points to the network's real warming pattern.  Each wrong choice either dismisses temperature entirely or claims a match the passage does not support.

items.stem: Choose the three true facts about how the three proposals measure up against Command's constraints.
choices: Proposal A treats the survival gap each season instead of closing it for good.
Proposal A requires authority the Network does not currently have.
Proposal B is too expensive to fit inside this year's field budget.
Proposal B satisfies the time and cost limits but does not fix the actual food gap.
Proposal C could take longer than Command's one-season window to even be decided.
Proposal C is guaranteed to arrive before the chicks' hungriest stretch next season.

distractorRationale.2: The report says the fencing itself is inexpensive, well inside the cost limit Command set.

The three wrong choices each invert a specific constraint the report states about a different proposal.

Second, the response must cost less than this year's field budget for Halyard Point.

The other two sentences add a supporting detail about emergency funding and describe the operative's overall task, neither one a constraint statement itself.

The other two sentences each describe a strength, fast setup, for a different proposal, not a flaw.

budget
authority

distractorRationale.1: Budget is the limit named in Command's second constraint, the cost limit, not the third constraint about authority.

items.quote: Third, the response must use only authority the Network already holds.

Time and budget each name one of the other two constraints, the one-season window and the cost limit, not this third one.

items.stem: What is Command's FIRST constraint on the response, the one it states before cost or authority?
choices: The response must cost less than this year's field budget for Halyard Point.
The response must use only authority the Network already holds.
The response must be approved by the fishery authority before it can begin.
The response must show a real effect on chick survival within one nesting season.

distractorRationale.1: Command lists this as its third constraint, the authority limit, not the first one it names.

items.explain: Command sets its constraints in a stated order, and the report names the time limit first: the response must show a real effect on chick survival within one nesting season, before it goes on to state the cost limit second and the authority limit third.

items.stem: Suppose a fourth proposal called for the Network to seek new region-wide fishery regulation that would move the herring season's start date permanently.  Based on the report's own reasoning about Proposal C, would this new idea likely satisfy Command's authority constraint?
choices: No, since it would still depend on a fishery authority that does not answer to the Network, the same problem Proposal C already has.
Yes, since a permanent regulation change is always more powerful than a one-time petition.
Yes, since region-wide regulation falls outside any single fishery authority's control.
There is no way to know without more information about the fishery authority.

distractorRationale.1: The permanence of the change does not touch the actual constraint.  The report's problem with Proposal C is which authority controls the decision, not how long the decision would last.
distractorRationale.2: The report describes the fishery authority as the body that decides herring-season timing.  A region-wide version of that same request would still need that same authority's approval, not less of it.
distractorRationale.3: The report already gives the needed information: the fishery authority does not answer to the Network and no petition has ever been decided in under four months, both of which apply just as directly to a bigger, region-wide version of the same request.

items.explain: The report's actual objection to Proposal C is that the fishery authority does not answer to the Network and could take months longer than Command's one-season window to decide, a problem tied to WHO controls the decision, not to the size or permanence of what is being asked for, so a bigger regional version of the same request would run into the identical authority and timing problem.

items.stem: The colony's survival problem began as a shift in the terns' own nesting timing, driven by warming spring air, and it eventually showed up as a falling fledge rate in the chicks.  Using the field manual's own vocabulary, which word best names the way a change in one part led to a change in a different, connected part?
choices: component
interaction
system
subsystem

distractorRationale.0: Component names one small physical part, not the connection between a timing shift in one species and a survival change in another.
distractorRationale.2: System names a whole set of parts working toward one job, not the specific ripple connecting one change to another.
distractorRationale.3: Subsystem names one smaller system nested inside a bigger one, not the event of one part's change causing a connected part to change too.

items.explain: The field manual defines an interaction as what happens when one part changes and a connected part changes with it, exactly the shape of the colony's own mystery: the terns' own nesting timing shifted twenty-eight days earlier, driven by warming spring air, and that shift rippled into chicks hatching weeks before their food arrives and a falling fledge rate, the same vocabulary word tile one introduces on a station's own life-support system.

items.stem: In eight words or fewer, name the one proposal that both fits every one of Command's constraints and actually treats the chicks' food gap.
accept: proposal a, the temporary feeding station
items.explain: Proposal A fits inside Command's time and cost limits and needs no new authority, and unlike Proposal B, it directly targets the chicks' actual problem, the food gap the nesting record identified, by stocking fish through the exact three-week window before the herring arrive, even though it must be repeated each season rather than closing the gap for good.

partA.stem: In this manual, what does the word boundary mean?
choices: A line somebody draws to mark what belongs to a system and what does not.
A wall or seal built around a station to keep the weather outside it.
The smallest piece inside a subsystem, small enough for a technician to repair.
Anything that crosses into a system from outside of it.

partB.stem: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer you just gave?
choices: A sealed station draws its line so that no matter crosses in either direction, though sunlight still crosses that boundary going in and the day's readings still go out by radio.
A boundary marks what counts as part of the system, and everything else counts as outside it.
Anything crossing the boundary on its way in is an input, and anything crossing on its way out is an output.
The filter membrane sits inside the line, so the membrane is a component rather than an input.

distractorRationale.1: A sealed station is one example of a boundary drawn very tightly, not the definition of the word.  The manual says a boundary is a line marking what is inside a system, whether or not anything is actually built along it.
distractorRationale.2: That is a component.  The manual uses the filter membrane to show what sits INSIDE a boundary, which is the opposite of what the word boundary names.
distractorRationale.3: That is an input.  An input is defined by its relationship to the boundary, so it cannot also be the boundary itself.

items.explain: The manual defines a boundary as the line marking what counts as part of the system, with everything else counting as outside it.  Inputs, outputs, and components are all defined by where they sit relative to that line, so none of them can be the line.

partA.stem: Why is the crew quarters' damp air an input under one boundary and not an input at all under a wider one?
choices: The crew produces less damp air once the whole life-support system is running.
Moving the line changes what crosses it, and only things that cross it can be inputs.
Damp air is really a component rather than an input.
The water subsystem is the only subsystem sitting inside life support.

partB.stem: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer you just gave?
choices: Now draw the boundary around all of life support instead, with the whole crew inside the larger line.
The filter membrane sits inside the line, so the membrane is a component rather than an input.
Draw the boundary around that one subsystem, and damp air from the crew quarters becomes an input, while clean water sent back to the taps becomes an output.
That same damp air never crosses the new boundary at all, because water is only moving from one subsystem to the next.

distractorRationale.0: Nothing in the manual says the amount of damp air changes.  What changes is where the line is drawn, and therefore whether that air crosses it.
distractorRationale.2: The membrane is the component in this example, not the damp air.  A component sits inside the line; damp air is something that either crosses a line or does not.
distractorRationale.3: The manual never claims water is the only subsystem inside life support.  It uses the water subsystem as one example of a smaller line drawn inside a bigger one.

items.explain: Under the narrow line, the damp air comes from the crew quarters outside the water subsystem, so it crosses in and counts as an input.  Under the wider line the crew is inside too, so that air never crosses anything, and water is simply moving from one subsystem to the next.

partA.stem: According to the manual, what makes the handoff between two subsystems an interaction?
choices: The two subsystems are repaired by the same technician.
The two subsystems sit inside the same sealed station.
One subsystem's output is the next one's input, so a change in one reaches the other.
An operative tracing the ripple through the station is what creates it.

partB.stem: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer you just gave?
choices: The output of one subsystem is usually the input of the subsystem beside it, and that handoff is what the manual calls an interaction.
A sealed station draws its line so that no matter crosses in either direction, though sunlight still crosses that boundary going in and the day's readings still go out by radio.
Trace the handoffs through a station and an operative has traced the ripple.
A report naming the wrong boundary sends a technician into the wrong room.

distractorRationale.0: The manual mentions a technician only to warn about being sent to the wrong room.  Who does the repair has nothing to do with whether two subsystems interact.
distractorRationale.1: Sharing a station is not enough.  The manual defines the interaction by the handoff itself, where one subsystem's output becomes another subsystem's input.
distractorRationale.3: Tracing is how an operative FINDS an interaction.  The handoff is already happening whether or not anybody has traced it yet.

items.explain: The manual names the handoff itself as the interaction: the output of one subsystem is usually the input of the subsystem beside it, which is exactly how a change in one part reaches a different part.  Repair crews, shared buildings, and tracing are all things that happen around an interaction rather than things that make one.

partA.stem: What does the manual say still crosses the boundary of a sealed station?
choices: Nothing at all crosses it, which is what the word sealed means.
Water and air cross it as they move between the station's subsystems.
Components cross it whenever a technician swaps a worn part out.
Energy and information, even though solid, liquid, and gas cannot.

partB.stem: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer you just gave?
choices: A sealed station draws its line so that no matter crosses in either direction, though sunlight still crosses that boundary going in and the day's readings still go out by radio.
The filter membrane sits inside the line, so the membrane is a component rather than an input.
Energy and information cross a seal that solid, liquid, and gas cannot.
That same damp air never crosses the new boundary at all, because water is only moving from one subsystem to the next.

distractorRationale.0: That is the manual's first half taken for the whole of it.  The manual does say no matter crosses in either direction, and then it says sunlight still crosses going in and the day's readings still go out by radio, so "nothing at all" stops being true before the sentence ends.
distractorRationale.1: Water and air move between subsystems INSIDE the line.  Moving from one subsystem to the next is exactly what not crossing the outer boundary looks like.
distractorRationale.2: The manual never describes parts being carried in or out of a sealed station.  A component is described as sitting inside the line, not as something that crosses one.

items.explain: The manual is specific about what a seal does and does not stop: no matter crosses in either direction, but sunlight still crosses going in and the day's readings still go out by radio.  Energy and information cross a seal that solid, liquid, and gas cannot, which is how a sealed station can send anything home at all.

items.stem: Choose the three statements that match how this manual uses the words boundary, input, and output.
choices: A boundary is a line drawn to mark what counts as part of a system.
An input is any part a technician can pull out and replace on its own.
Anything crossing the boundary on its way out of the system is an output.
Moving the boundary makes no difference to what counts as an input.
A sealed boundary stops sunlight and radio signals along with everything else.
One subsystem's output can be the next subsystem's input.

distractorRationale.1: That describes a component.  An input is something crossing the boundary on its way in, not a part sitting inside the line waiting to be replaced.
distractorRationale.3: The manual says the opposite.  Move the line and the same water or the same air changes names entirely, because what crosses the boundary changes with it.
distractorRationale.4: A seal stops matter, not energy or information.  The manual says sunlight still crosses going in and the day's readings still go out by radio.

items.explain: The three correct statements are the manual's own three definitions: the boundary is the line, an output is whatever crosses it going out, and the handoff where one subsystem's output becomes the next one's input is what the manual calls an interaction.  Each wrong choice either confuses a component with an input or denies something the manual states directly.

items.stem: Tap the two sentences that together show the same damp air counting as an input under one boundary and not crossing at all under a wider one.
spans: Perrin uses the training bay's own water subsystem to show operatives how it works.
Draw the boundary around that one subsystem, and damp air from the crew quarters becomes an input, while clean water sent back to the taps becomes an output.
The filter membrane sits inside the line, so the membrane is a component rather than an input.
Now draw the boundary around all of life support instead, with the whole crew inside the larger line.
That same damp air never crosses the new boundary at all, because water is only moving from one subsystem to the next.
items.explain: The pair of sentences is the manual's whole demonstration: under the narrow line the crew quarters sit outside, so their damp air crosses in and counts as an input, while under the wider line the crew is inside and that same air crosses nothing.  The other three sentences set the example up or describe the membrane, without showing the same air changing status.

items.stem: Tap the two sentences that state what a sealed boundary stops and what still gets through it.
spans: A report naming the wrong boundary sends a technician into the wrong room.
Some boundaries are drawn far tighter than others.
A sealed station draws its line so that no matter crosses in either direction, though sunlight still crosses that boundary going in and the day's readings still go out by radio.
Energy and information cross a seal that solid, liquid, and gas cannot.
Perrin says most crews forget that difference by about the fourth day.
items.explain: One sentence gives the seal's limit in both directions and names sunlight and the day's readings as the exceptions, and the next states the rule behind those exceptions in general terms.  The other three introduce the topic, warn about naming the wrong boundary, or comment on how quickly crews forget, none of which says what a seal actually stops.

items.stem: Anything crossing the boundary on its way in is an {{0}}, and anything crossing on its way out is an output.

choices: output
input
component

distractorRationale.0: An output is what crosses on its way OUT, which this same sentence names at its end.  The blank sits in the half of the sentence about crossing in.
distractorRationale.2: A component is a part sitting inside the boundary, like the filter membrane.  A component does not cross the line at all, and the blank is about something that does.

items.quote: Anything crossing the boundary on its way in is an input, and anything crossing on its way out is an output.
items.explain: The manual defines both words in one sentence by direction of travel: whatever crosses the boundary on the way in is an input, and whatever crosses on the way out is an output.  The other half of the sentence gives the answer away to anyone who reads it, since output is already named there, and a component never crosses the line in either direction.

items.stem: An operative redraws a boundary so the crew quarters now fall inside it.  What does the movement of that damp air become under the new line?
choices: An output, since the air now leaves the water subsystem behind.
A component of the water subsystem.
An interaction, since it is now a handoff between two subsystems inside the line.
Nothing the manual names, because movement inside a line goes uncounted.

distractorRationale.0: An output is something crossing the boundary on its way OUT.  With the crew inside the line, that air crosses nothing at all, so it is neither an input nor an output.
distractorRationale.1: A component is a repairable part sitting inside a boundary, like the filter membrane.  Movement between subsystems is not a part, however far the line is redrawn.
distractorRationale.3: The manual names it directly.  The output of one subsystem is usually the input of the subsystem beside it, and that handoff is what it calls an interaction.

items.explain: Redrawing the line does more than rename the air.  Under the narrow boundary the damp air crossed in as an input and clean water crossed out as an output;  under the wider one neither crosses anything, and what is left is water moving from one subsystem to the next.  The manual has a word for that handoff, and the word is interaction.

items.stem: According to the manual, which of these can cross the boundary of a sealed station?
choices: Radio signals carrying the day's readings out.
Water piped in from outside the dome.
Replacement filter membranes brought in by supply run.
Air vented in from the outside atmosphere.

distractorRationale.1: A sealed line stops matter in both directions, and water is matter.  The manual names solid, liquid and gas together as what a seal stops.
distractorRationale.2: A membrane is a solid object, and no matter crosses a seal.  The manual lists only energy and information as getting through.
distractorRationale.3: Gas is matter too, and the seal stops it exactly as it stops liquids and solids.  Sunlight and radio are the exceptions, not air.

items.explain: The manual is precise about what a seal does and does not stop: no matter crosses in either direction, while sunlight still crosses going in and the day's readings still go out by radio.  Energy and information cross a seal that solid, liquid and gas cannot, which is why a sealed station can still report home.

items.stem: An operative files a report reading only "the water system failed."  Using Instructor Perrin's rule, what is missing?
choices: The exact time the failure was first noticed.
How many crew members the failure affected.
Whether the station is sealed or open to the outside.
Which line the trouble sits inside, so a technician knows where to go.

distractorRationale.0: Perrin's rule is about naming the boundary, not the timing.  A time stamp still would not tell a technician which room to walk into.
distractorRationale.1: Nothing in the manual asks for a headcount.  The rule is about locating the failure, not measuring how far it reached.
distractorRationale.2: How tightly the OUTER boundary is drawn says nothing about where a fault sits inside the station.  The report still has to name that line.

items.explain: Perrin's rule is to name the boundary before naming the failure, because "the water system failed" could mean a component, a subsystem, or the handoff between two of them.  Until the report says which line the trouble sits inside, nobody knows which room to send a technician to, and the report has named nothing yet.

items.stem: The manual traces damp air through the training bay's water subsystem.  Put these four stages in the order the manual gives them.
tiles: The filter membrane, a component inside the line, does its work
Damp air sits in the crew quarters, outside the subsystem's line
Clean water is piped back to the taps as an output
The damp air crosses the boundary and counts as an input
items.explain: The sequence follows the manual's own example from outside the line inward and back out again: the air starts outside the water subsystem, crosses the boundary and becomes an input, meets the filter membrane sitting inside as a component, and leaves as clean water, which is the subsystem's output.  Getting the middle two the wrong way round is the common slip, since a component is easy to mistake for an input.

partA.stem: Why does this order leave the water subsystem and the food modules off it entirely?
choices: Dust on a clear panel cannot affect a job that never depended on light passing through.
Both of them had already been cleaned earlier in the same week.
Both of them had failed, so a cleaning order would not have helped either one.
Only one operative was free that morning, so the order had to stay short.

partB.stem: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer you just gave?
choices: One operative, about twenty minutes.
Dust on a clear panel cannot reach a job that never depended on light getting through in the first place.
The dome's maintenance log had recorded no scheduled cleaning of any kind since the seal closed.
Water reclamation has held near ninety-five percent through the whole drift, and the food modules have covered every meal.

distractorRationale.1: The log records no scheduled cleaning of any kind since the seal closed, so nothing on the dome had been cleaned recently, those two subsystems included.
distractorRationale.2: Neither subsystem failed.  Water reclamation held near ninety-five percent and the food modules covered every meal, right through the drift.
distractorRationale.3: One operative for about twenty minutes is the size of the panel job itself.  It is not the reason two working subsystems were left off the order.

items.explain: The order draws a line around what the evidence actually reached: dust sitting on a clear panel can only affect a job that depends on light getting through that panel.  Water reclamation and the food modules both kept working through the whole drift, so an order sending a crew after them would waste a morning on subsystems the evidence already cleared.

partA.stem: According to the order, what has to happen before the order can be closed?
choices: The panel has to be wiped with the dry cloth and then the damp one.
A later status log has to show the oxygen reading climbing back toward twenty and a half percent.
Somebody has to be named as the owner of the two-week cleaning task.
Network Command has to file its own second copy of the order.

partB.stem: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer you just gave?
choices: Panel cleaning becomes a two-week task on the dome's maintenance board, carrying an owner's name beside it the same as every other task.
Filed by Dr. Renata Kessler, systems lead, on the morning after the walk-through, with Network Command holding the second copy.
The order closes only if that log shows oxygen climbing back toward twenty and a half percent, which was the reading the dome held on day ninety before any of this started.
Wipe down the clear roof panel above the algae bioreactor, dry cloth first and damp cloth second.

distractorRationale.0: That is the work the order requires, and the order says outright that it does not close on the morning the panel comes clean.  A clean panel is effort; the order closes on evidence.
distractorRationale.2: Naming an owner is part of the new standing schedule, which exists to stop the problem coming back.  The order itself closes on the oxygen reading.
distractorRationale.3: Command holding a second copy is simply how the order gets filed.  The order names one closing condition, and it is about the dome's oxygen reading.

items.explain: The order separates the work from the proof: wiping the panel is the effort, and the oxygen reading climbing back toward twenty and a half percent in Dr. Kessler's next log is the evidence.  Until that log arrives on day one hundred forty-six, nobody knows whether the fix actually worked.

partA.stem: The order says nothing inside the dome had broken.  What does it name as the actual failure?
choices: A piece of gear running well outside the limits it was built for.
The bioreactor's clear roof panel cracking after one hundred eighteen days.
A cleaning job that was never put on anybody's schedule.
The dome staying sealed for longer than it was ever designed to stay sealed.

partB.stem: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer you just gave?
choices: That panel is the bioreactor's one component whose job depends on light crossing a clear surface, and dust had been settling on it since the day the dome sealed.
The failure was a job that never got scheduled, and no sensor anywhere on the dome reports that kind.
Nothing inside the dome had broken, and every piece of gear was working exactly as it was built to work.
One hundred eighteen days is a long time for a job to belong to no one.

distractorRationale.0: The order says the opposite: every piece of gear was working exactly as it was built to work.  The failure was not in the equipment at all.
distractorRationale.1: The panel was never damaged.  What sat on it was dust, so the trouble was light not getting through rather than the panel itself giving way.
distractorRationale.3: The order calls one hundred eighteen days a long time for a JOB to belong to nobody, which is about the missing schedule.  It never suggests the seal itself ran too long.

items.explain: Every piece of gear on the dome was working exactly as built, which is what makes this failure hard to catch: it was a job nobody had been assigned, and no sensor on the dome reports an unassigned job.  The equipment answers were all wrong because the equipment was never the problem.

partA.stem: Why does the order turn panel cleaning into a standing task with an owner's name beside it?
choices: Because wiping the panel is too large a job for a single operative.
Because the dome's other subsystems need the same two-week cleaning.
Because Dr. Kessler files a status log every four weeks.
Because a task belonging to nobody does not get done, which is how the dust built up.

partB.stem: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer you just gave?
choices: A task nobody owns is a task nobody does.
One operative, about twenty minutes.
Dr. Kessler's next status log falls four weeks after her last one, on day one hundred forty-six.
Neither subsystem appears on this order, and neither belongs on it.

distractorRationale.0: The order sizes the job at one operative for about twenty minutes.  It is small work; the problem was that nobody had been assigned to do it.
distractorRationale.1: The order deliberately leaves the other subsystems off, saying neither belongs on it.  The new schedule covers the panel.
distractorRationale.2: The four-week log cadence is how the fix gets verified afterward.  It is not the reason the cleaning task needed an owner in the first place.

items.explain: The dust built up over twenty-eight straight days because no cleaning had ever been scheduled, and the order fixes the cause rather than only the symptom by giving the task a fixed interval and a named owner.  A task nobody owns is a task nobody does, however small and however obvious it looks afterward.

items.stem: Choose the three statements this maintenance order actually makes.
choices: The bioreactor's equipment had failed and now needs replacing.
Dust blocking light is what slowed the algae down.
The water subsystem and the food modules both stay off this order.
The order closes as soon as the panel has been wiped clean.
Panel cleaning becomes a repeating task with somebody's name on it.
The drift is a sign of a change happening across the whole network.

distractorRationale.0: The order says nothing inside the dome had broken and every piece of gear was working exactly as built.  Nothing is being replaced.
distractorRationale.3: The order says it does not close on the morning the panel comes clean.  It closes only once a later log shows the oxygen reading climbing back.
distractorRationale.5: Nothing in the order points outside the dome.  The cause it names is dust on one panel inside this one station, traced across twenty-eight straight days of buildup.

items.explain: The order makes three claims and no more: dust on the clear panel starved the algae of light, the two working subsystems stay off the order because the evidence cleared them, and cleaning becomes a scheduled task with an owner.  The wrong choices each add something the order rules out, whether broken gear, an early close, or a cause reaching beyond this one dome.

items.stem: Tap the two sentences that show WHY the water subsystem and the food modules are cleared.
spans: Water reclamation has held near ninety-five percent through the whole drift, and the food modules have covered every meal.
Neither subsystem appears on this order, and neither belongs on it.
Dust on a clear panel cannot reach a job that never depended on light getting through in the first place.
An order that sends a crew after subsystems the evidence already cleared wastes a working morning.
Panel cleaning becomes a two-week task on the dome's maintenance board, carrying an owner's name beside it the same as every other task.
items.explain: One sentence reports what the two subsystems actually did through the drift, and the other gives the reason dust on a light-admitting panel could never have reached them;  together those are the evidence.  Leaving the subsystems off the order, and warning about wasted mornings, are conclusions drawn FROM that evidence, and the cleaning schedule is a separate matter entirely.

items.stem: Tap the three sentences that show this order closes on a measured result rather than on the work being finished.
spans: A task nobody owns is a task nobody does.
This order does not close on the morning the panel comes clean.
Dr. Kessler's next status log falls four weeks after her last one, on day one hundred forty-six.
The order closes only if that log shows oxygen climbing back toward twenty and a half percent, which was the reading the dome held on day ninety before any of this started.
A clean panel is effort, and a recovered reading is evidence.
items.explain: The three sentences state the closing rule from three directions: what does not close the order, what does, and the principle underneath both.  The sentence about unowned tasks explains why the dust built up in the first place, and the filing date only says when the evidence will arrive, neither of which is the condition the order closes on.

items.stem: A clean panel is effort, and a recovered reading is {{0}}.

choices: effort
maintenance
evidence

distractorRationale.0: The sentence has already used effort, for the clean panel itself.  The blank has to name what the recovered reading gives that a clean panel does not.
distractorRationale.1: Maintenance is the work being done, which is the effort half of this sentence.  The blank names the proof that the work actually succeeded.

items.quote: A clean panel is effort, and a recovered reading is evidence.
items.explain: The order draws a line between doing the job and proving the job worked: wiping the panel is effort, and only the oxygen reading climbing back in a later log is evidence.  That is why the order stays open until day one hundred forty-six rather than closing on the morning the panel comes clean, and it is the reason a sensor cannot report the failure that caused all this.

items.stem: Under the new standing schedule, how often must the bioreactor's roof panel be cleaned?
choices: Every four weeks, matching Dr. Kessler's filing cadence.
Every two weeks, as a task carrying an owner's name.
Once, as soon as this order is issued.
Whenever a sensor reports the oxygen reading falling.

distractorRationale.0: Four weeks is how often Dr. Kessler files her status log.  The cleaning task is deliberately set to a shorter interval than the reporting one.
distractorRationale.2: A single cleaning is the work the order requires now.  The standing schedule exists precisely so the job repeats instead of happening once and lapsing again.
distractorRationale.3: The order says no sensor on the dome reports an unscheduled job at all, which is why the cleaning goes on a fixed interval rather than waiting for a reading to move.

items.explain: The order turns panel cleaning into a two-week task on the maintenance board with an owner's name beside it, because the whole failure was a job nobody had been assigned.  A fixed interval and a named owner are what stop a task from belonging to no one for another hundred and eighteen days.

items.stem: Suppose the panel is wiped clean but the day-one-hundred-forty-six log still shows oxygen at nineteen and a half percent.  What does this order say should happen?
choices: The order closes anyway, since the required work was completed.
The water subsystem should be cleaned next.
The order stays open, because it closes on the reading rather than on the work.
The dome should be unsealed to let outside air in.

distractorRationale.0: The order says outright that it does not close on the morning the panel comes clean.  A clean panel is effort;  a recovered reading is the evidence.
distractorRationale.1: The order clears the water subsystem by name, since dust on a light-admitting panel could never reach a job that does not depend on light getting through.
distractorRationale.3: Nothing in the order contemplates breaking the seal.  An unrecovered reading would mean the cause has not been found, not that the dome needs opening.

items.explain: The order separates doing the job from proving the job worked, and it closes only on the second.  If the reading has not climbed back toward twenty and a half percent by the next log, then dust on the panel was not the whole cause, and the dome's oxygen drift is still unexplained.

items.stem: Why could the dome's own instruments not report the failure this order describes?
choices: Instruments measure quantities, and a job nobody scheduled is not one.
The sensors had been coated by the same layer of dust.
The bioreactor has no sensor of its own to report with.
The drift was too small for any instrument to detect.

distractorRationale.1: Nothing in the order says any sensor was dirty.  It states that every piece of gear was working exactly as it was built to work.
distractorRationale.2: The bioreactor's own daily readings are what drew attention in the first place, so it is measured.  What no instrument measures is whether a task was ever assigned.
distractorRationale.3: The instruments detected the drift clearly, from twenty and a half percent down to nineteen and a half.  What they could not report was why it was happening.

items.explain: Every piece of gear on the dome was working as built, which is what makes this failure hard to catch: the missing thing was a scheduled task, and no sensor anywhere measures whether a job has an owner.  That is exactly why the fix is a schedule with a name on it rather than a new instrument.

items.stem: Match each section of this maintenance order to what that section actually specifies.
colLabels: A two-week interval with an owner's name beside it
A dry cloth and then a damp one over the bioreactor's roof panel
A later log showing oxygen climbing back toward twenty and a half percent
items.explain: The order separates three different things a maintenance document has to carry: the work itself, the evidence that will close it, and the schedule that stops the problem recurring.  Reading the verification row as the cleaning is the usual slip, since both belong to the same repair, but a clean panel is effort while a recovered oxygen reading is the proof the effort worked.

partA.stem: Amaro notes that the air arriving behind the front was cold and very dry.  What does he read that as telling him?
choices: That the air mass had been sitting over cold land before it reached the relay.
That the air mass had crossed warm open ocean, which dried it out on the way.
That the front had stalled over the headland and stopped moving.
That the relay's humidity instrument had failed during the night.

partB.stem: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer you just gave?
choices: The temperature climbed to seventy degrees, and the humidity rose to sixty-one percent.
The temperature read forty-nine degrees, the coldest morning of the week, and the humidity dropped to thirty-eight percent.
The barometer had climbed back to twenty-nine and nine tenths inches and was still rising.
The air that came in behind the front was cold and very dry, which is the mark of an air mass that has been sitting over cold land.

distractorRationale.1: Air sitting over warm ocean water picks moisture up rather than losing it, so an ocean crossing is not what would have dried this air out.  The warmer, moister readings that might suggest an ocean came on the second morning, ahead of the front rather than behind it, and the direction a wind arrives from does not by itself name where its air has been.
distractorRationale.2: Rising pressure and a clearing sky are the marks of a front that has passed through, not of one sitting still overhead.
distractorRationale.3: The humidity drop agrees with every other reading that morning: the coldest temperature of the week, rising pressure, a clear sky.  A broken instrument would not line up with all three.

items.explain: An air mass takes on the temperature and moisture of whatever it has been sitting over, so cold and dry together point back to cold land as the source region.  Amaro is reading the air's own properties rather than guessing from the direction it arrived from.

partA.stem: What does Amaro's closing note say about the direction the wind turned during this front?
choices: It turned the opposite way round from the last front the relay logged.
It turned in the same order it always turns at this relay.
It held steady out of the southwest for the whole week.
It only began shifting after the heaviest rain had already fallen.

partB.stem: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer you just gave?
choices: The front that crossed the headland this week moved faster than the last one.
Heavy rain fell all afternoon.
The wind turned the way it always turns here, southwest to west to northwest to north.
The wind came from the southwest again, harder than the day before.

distractorRationale.0: The only comparison Amaro draws with the last front is its speed.  The turning order is the thing he describes as always the same here.
distractorRationale.2: The southwest wind lasted two mornings.  By the third the wind had shifted to the west, and by the fifth it was coming from the north.
distractorRationale.3: The wind had already shifted to the west on the third morning, before the fourth morning's heavy rain.  The turning began ahead of the worst weather rather than after it.

items.explain: Amaro records the wind moving southwest to west to northwest to north, and says explicitly that this is the way it always turns at Halyard Point.  A consistent turning order is what makes the wind reading useful as a signal rather than just another number that moved.

items.stem: Choose the three fifth-morning readings that show the front had already passed the relay.
choices: The barometer had climbed back to twenty-nine and nine tenths inches.
The barometer reached its lowest reading of the whole week.
Humidity had dropped to thirty-eight percent.
The temperature was the coldest of the week.
Humidity reached ninety-one percent.
The wind was blowing at thirty-four miles per hour.

distractorRationale.1: The lowest reading of the week was twenty-nine and three tenths inches, on the FOURTH morning.  By the fifth the barometer had climbed back to twenty-nine and nine tenths and was still rising.
distractorRationale.4: Ninety-one percent was the fourth morning's humidity, with the rain falling hard.  On the fifth morning the humidity had dropped to thirty-eight percent.
distractorRationale.5: Thirty-four miles per hour was the fourth morning's wind.  By the fifth the wind had eased to eighteen miles per hour and had come round to the north.

items.explain: The fifth morning reads the opposite way from the fourth on every count: pressure climbing instead of bottoming out, humidity down to thirty-eight percent instead of up at ninety-one, and the coldest air of the week arriving behind the front rather than ahead of it.  Each wrong choice is a real reading from the log taken from the wrong morning, which is the fourth, when the front was still overhead.

partA.stem: Under the standing procedure, why is one falling barometer reading not enough to issue a warning?
choices: The barometer is the least reliable of the four instruments a relay tracks.
Pressure has to be checked against the colony's nest count first.
Pressure can drop for an hour and climb straight back, so one reading proves nothing.
A warning may only go out in the twelve hours after a reading falls.

partB.stem: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer you just gave?
choices: The warning goes out at least twelve hours before the front is expected to arrive.
A single reading is never a warning by itself, because a barometer can fall for an hour and climb right back afterward.
The colony line belongs at the bottom of the page and stays out of the warning decision entirely.
An officer watching a barometer fall is the worst possible person to be deciding what a falling barometer means.

distractorRationale.0: The procedure never calls the barometer unreliable.  It says the officer watching it is badly placed to judge it in the moment, which is why the rule is written down beforehand.
distractorRationale.1: The procedure keeps the colony line out of the warning decision entirely.  It is never used as a check on anything.
distractorRationale.3: The twelve hours run the other way.  The warning must go out at least twelve hours BEFORE the front is expected, so that boats can still act on it.

items.explain: A single reading can move and move back, which is ordinary weather rather than a signal, so the procedure requires at least two of the four readings to move together from one morning to the next.  The rule is about how many independent readings agree, not about which instrument is trusted.

partA.stem: The procedure says a correct call made from the wrong readings is still a bad call.  What is the reasoning behind that?
choices: Officers who guess correctly get rewarded and stop following the procedure.
The weather that follows a call is the only fair test of that call.
Readings that did not support the call should be left out of the file.
A call that got lucky teaches nothing, and the same reasoning will fail somebody else later.

partB.stem: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer you just gave?
choices: File the readings that supported the call alongside the readings that did not.
The procedure leans toward calling it early on purpose.
A call gets judged on the log rather than on the weather that happened to follow.
A correct call made from the wrong readings is still a bad call, and somebody with worse luck will make it again next month.

distractorRationale.0: The procedure leans early to protect boats and says nothing about rewarding anybody.  Its concern is the reasoning behind a call, not who gets credit for one.
distractorRationale.1: The procedure says the opposite: a call gets judged on the log rather than on the weather that happened to follow it.
distractorRationale.2: The procedure requires both kinds of reading to be filed together.  Leaving the unsupportive ones out is exactly what it forbids.

items.explain: Judging a call by its outcome rewards luck and hides bad reasoning, so the procedure judges the log instead: what did the readings show, and did they meet the rule.  Reasoning that happened to work once will be used again by somebody whose luck runs out, which is why a lucky call still counts as a bad one.

items.stem: Tap the two sentences that state when the warning went out and how much lead time it bought.
spans: Thin high cloud covered the horizon before midday.
Amaro sent the coast warning out on this morning's readings.
Rain began before midday and kept on into the evening.
Officer Amaro's closing note runs three lines.
The warning had gone out a full day before the first rain.
items.explain: One sentence puts the warning on the second morning and the other measures the lead time it bought, a full day ahead of the first rain.  The cloud and the rain are what the warning was about rather than a statement of when it went out or how much warning it gave, and the line about the note's length says nothing about timing at all.

items.stem: Tap the two sentences that state the two-reading rule itself, rather than an example of it or a different rule.
spans: At least two of the four tracked readings must move together, from one morning to the next.
Pressure falling while humidity climbs will satisfy the rule, and so will pressure falling while the wind both shifts direction and strengthens.
One reading moving on one morning does not satisfy it, however sharply that reading happened to move.
The warning goes out at least twelve hours before the front is expected to arrive.
A warning arriving alongside the rain is not a warning at all.
items.explain: A rule and an example of a rule are different things, and this pair is the rule: what must happen for a warning to be justified, and what explicitly does not count.  The sentence about pressure and humidity gives two illustrations of the rule being met, while the twelve-hour sentences belong to a separate rule about timing.

items.stem: The air that came in behind the front was cold and very dry, which is the mark of an air mass that has been sitting over {{0}}.

choices: warm ocean
cold land
open water

distractorRationale.0: Air sitting over warm ocean water turns warm and picks moisture up as it travels.  The air Amaro logged arrived cold and very dry, which is the opposite on both counts.
distractorRationale.2: Open water is where an air mass collects moisture rather than loses it.  This air reached the relay at thirty-eight percent humidity, the driest reading of the week.

items.quote: The air that came in behind the front was cold and very dry, which is the mark of an air mass that has been sitting over cold land.
items.explain: An air mass takes on the temperature and the moisture of whatever it has been sitting over, so its own readings point back to where it came from.  Cold and very dry together points to cold land, which is why Amaro can name a likely source without knowing anything about what lies in the direction the wind arrived from.

items.stem: Why could Amaro not have issued the coast warning on the first morning of week eleven?
choices: The barometer had not yet reached its lowest point.
The colony count had not been filed for the week yet.
The wind had not yet swung round to the north.
Nothing had moved yet, and a first morning has no morning before it to compare against.

distractorRationale.0: The rule never waits for the lowest reading.  By the time pressure bottoms out the front has arrived, which is far too late for the warning to help anybody.
distractorRationale.1: The colony line stays out of the warning decision entirely, whichever morning it happens to be filed on.
distractorRationale.2: The wind reaches north on the fifth morning, after the front has passed.  Waiting for it would put the warning several days late.

items.explain: On the first morning the barometer read thirty and two tenths, humidity sat at forty-four percent, and the sky stayed clear, so nothing had moved in any direction.  The standing procedure needs at least two of the four readings moving together from one morning to the next, and a first morning has nothing behind it to compare against however good its readings look.

items.stem: A different relay logs a sharp overnight pressure fall with nothing else moving.  Under the standing procedure, may it issue a warning?
choices: Yes, because a sharp fall is the strongest single signal a relay gets.
No, since one reading on one morning does not satisfy the rule, however sharply it moved.
Yes, provided the officer files the supporting readings afterward.
No, because warnings may only go out twelve hours before a front.

distractorRationale.0: The procedure says a single reading is never a warning by itself, and it adds that a sharp move does not change that.  A barometer can fall for an hour and climb right back.
distractorRationale.2: Filing the readings is required for every call, but it is what makes a call reviewable rather than what makes it justified.  The rule still has to be met first.
distractorRationale.3: Twelve hours is a minimum lead time, not a window that forbids anything earlier.  The procedure leans toward calling it early on purpose.

items.explain: The two-reading rule exists because a single instrument can move and move back, which is ordinary weather rather than a signal.  Two of the four readings moving together from one morning to the next is what separates a front from noise, and no amount of sharpness in one reading substitutes for a second reading agreeing with it.

items.stem: Why does Command's procedure deliberately lean toward calling a front early?
choices: Early warnings turn out to be correct more often than late ones.
Officers are judged on how many warnings they manage to issue.
A needless warning costs a harbor one day;  a late one costs boats and crews.
The four readings are easier to read early in the morning.

distractorRationale.0: The procedure never claims early calls are more accurate.  It weighs what each kind of mistake costs, not how often each kind happens.
distractorRationale.1: A call is judged on the log rather than on a count of warnings or on the weather that happened to follow it.
distractorRationale.3: Nothing in the procedure concerns what time of day an instrument is read.  The lean is about which mistake Command is willing to make more often.

items.explain: Two different mistakes are possible and they do not cost the same, which is the whole reason a policy can be tilted on purpose.  Emptying a harbor for a day that turns out calm is recoverable, while a warning arriving with the rain reaches boats already at sea, so Command accepts the cheaper mistake more often to make the expensive one rare.

items.stem: Put these four stages of week eleven in the order Officer Amaro logged them.
tiles: A light southwest wind blows under a clear sky
Cold, very dry air arrives and the barometer climbs back
Pressure falls, thin high cloud spreads, and the warning goes out
Heavy rain falls and the barometer reaches its lowest reading
items.explain: The week runs from calm to front to clearance: a clear first morning, then falling pressure with high cloud on the second, when the warning went out, then the fourth morning's heavy rain at the week's lowest pressure, and finally the cold dry air behind the front with the barometer climbing again.  Putting the dry air before the rain is the common slip, since dry weather sounds like the calm end rather than the far side of a storm.

partA.stem: According to this manual, which cause belongs with the rainfall column?
choices: Where the wind belt has already travelled, over open water or over dry land.
The current that runs along the Cairn Bay coastline.
Water changing temperature far more slowly than land does.
The size of the post's own ten-year average.

partB.stem: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer you just gave?
choices: In this pair, the current does not explain the rainfall, and the wind's path does not explain the swing.
Reading the rainfall column, the cause is the wind belt's path instead.
An average answers exactly one question, which is what an ordinary year looks like at this post.

Reading the temperature column, the cause is water and the current: water changes temperature far more slowly than land does, and a current runs along the Cairn Bay coastline, so the air above that coast stays inside a narrower band all year.

distractorRationale.1: The manual names this as the exact mistake to avoid: the current does not explain the rainfall.  The current belongs with the temperature column.
distractorRationale.2: Water's slow temperature change is one of the two causes the manual pairs with the TEMPERATURE column.  Pairing it with rainfall is the swap the manual warns about.
distractorRationale.3: An average summarises a column rather than causing it.  The manual asks which cause explains the column, and an average explains nothing by itself.

items.explain: The manual pairs each column with its own cause and says so explicitly: the wind belt's path over water or over land explains the rainfall, while water and the current explain the temperature range.  Swapping the two can still produce the right number for entirely the wrong reason, which is the mistake the next operative would inherit.

partA.stem: According to the manual, which record does a station's baseline come from?
choices: The ten-year averages of every post on the network added together.
That station's own thirty-year history, and no other post's.
The warmest year the station has ever recorded.
Whichever nearby post happens to keep the most complete records.

partB.stem: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer you just gave?
choices: A warm year at Cairn Bay never gets held up against a cold year at Sable Flats, because the two posts are not the same kind of place and the comparison would mean nothing at all.
A range is the distance between the highest reading and the lowest one.
Every post on the network files a ten-year table, and every operative is expected to be able to read one.
Each post is measured against its own thirty-year history.

distractorRationale.0: Every post files a ten-year table, but the manual never combines them into one network figure.  A baseline belongs to the station it describes.
distractorRationale.2: The highest reading is one end of the RANGE.  A baseline is the whole record a station gets compared against, not its single most extreme year.
distractorRationale.3: The manual rules that out directly.  A warm year at one post never gets held up against a cold year at another, because the two are not the same kind of place.

items.explain: A baseline is the station's own thirty-year record, which is what makes a comparison mean anything: a warm year at Cairn Bay measured against a cold year at Sable Flats would compare two different kinds of place and tell nobody anything.  Each post is measured against itself.

items.stem: Choose the three statements that follow this manual's own rules for reading a ten-year table.
choices: A post's baseline is set by comparing it against a neighbouring post.
An average says what an ordinary year looks like, not what any single year did.
The coastal current is what explains the difference in rainfall.
The wind belt's path over water or land explains the rainfall difference.
One unusual year does not move a ten-year average by much.
Two posts that share an average must share a range as well.

distractorRationale.0: The manual allows only a station's own thirty-year history as its baseline, because comparing two different kinds of place would mean nothing at all.
distractorRationale.2: That is the cross-pairing the manual warns about by name.  The current explains the temperature range; the wind belt's path explains the rainfall.
distractorRationale.5: The manual says two posts can share an average while sharing nothing else, and that the range is usually where the difference shows itself.

items.explain: The three correct statements are the manual's three working rules: an average describes an ordinary year rather than any real one, the rainfall column pairs with the wind belt's path, and a decade of averaging absorbs one strange year.  Sable Flats has logged a five-inch year and a fourteen-inch year with its ten-year average still holding near nine, which is that last rule measured.

partA.stem: Why does the briefing tell a Sable Flats transfer to pack for hard heat and hard cold both?
choices: Sable Flats is simply a harder posting than Cairn Bay is.
Rain at Sable Flats can arrive in any season without warning.
Its average high and average low sit sixty-eight degrees apart across one year.
One mid-weight kit already covers most of the year there.

partB.stem: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer you just gave?
choices: That is a spread of sixty-eight degrees across a single year.
Sable Flats averages nine inches of rain a year, while Cairn Bay averages forty-two.
One mid-weight kit covers most of a Cairn Bay year.
The kit differs because the year differs, not because one posting is harder than the other.

distractorRationale.0: The briefing says the kit differs because the year differs, not because one posting is harder than the other.
distractorRationale.1: Sable Flats averages nine inches of rain a year against Cairn Bay's forty-two.  The two-kit advice is about the temperature spread, not about rain.
distractorRationale.3: That line is about Cairn Bay, whose spread is thirty-three degrees.  It is the reason Cairn Bay needs one kit rather than two.

items.explain: Sable Flats averages a summer high of ninety-six degrees against a winter low of twenty-eight, so a single kit cannot cover both ends of its year.  Cairn Bay's spread is thirty-three degrees, roughly half as wide, which is why one mid-weight kit does the job there.

partA.stem: A transfer lands at Cairn Bay during a cold snap and packs for a cold year.  What does the briefing say is wrong with that?
choices: Cairn Bay never gets cold, so the transfer must have misread something.
The transfer should have packed for the wettest year on record instead.
Cold snaps at Cairn Bay are caused by the current along its coast.
The gear list follows the ten-year averages, not the weather on arrival day.

partB.stem: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer you just gave?
choices: Cairn Bay averages a summer high of seventy-four against a winter low of forty-one.
The steadiness at Cairn Bay comes from the open water beside it, whose temperature changes slowly, and from the current that runs along that coast.
The gear list follows the ten-year averages.
On the coast, storage is never the problem, but drying gear is.

distractorRationale.0: Cairn Bay does get cold, with an average winter low of forty-one degrees.  The mistake is judging a whole year by the week you happened to arrive in.
distractorRationale.1: Coastal packing is about drying gear rather than water storage, and the briefing points transfers at the averages rather than at any single extreme year.
distractorRationale.2: The current is named as the reason Cairn Bay stays STEADY across the year.  Using a long-term cause to explain one cold week mixes up climate and weather.

items.explain: One cold week is weather, and the briefing packs for climate: the gear list follows the ten-year averages rather than whatever the sky is doing on arrival day.  A transfer landing at Sable Flats during a wet spell would make the identical mistake in the opposite direction.

items.stem: Tap the two sentences that each pair one column of the table with its own correct cause.
spans: Now the part new operatives get wrong, which is the reason this page exists at all.
Match the cause to the column.

Reading the temperature column, the cause is water and the current: water changes temperature far more slowly than land does, and a current runs along the Cairn Bay coastline, so the air above that coast stays inside a narrower band all year.
Reading the rainfall column, the cause is the wind belt's path instead.
In this pair, the current does not explain the rainfall, and the wind's path does not explain the swing.
items.explain: The two keyed sentences are the pairings themselves, one per column, with the mechanism spelled out in each case.  The others introduce the section, give the instruction without carrying it out, or state the pairing negatively by naming the two swaps to avoid, which is useful but is not itself a pairing.

items.stem: Tap the two sentences that name a CAUSE of the difference between the two posts, rather than a consequence of it.
spans: Inland, the storage tanks are what matter, and every transfer learns the refill schedule in the first week.
The steadiness at Cairn Bay comes from the open water beside it, whose temperature changes slowly, and from the current that runs along that coast.
It comes from where the wind belt has already been before it arrives.
A transfer landing at Sable Flats during a wet spell will pack badly for the winter that follows.
The gear list follows the ten-year averages.
items.explain: The two keyed sentences name the mechanisms: the slow-changing water and the coastal current behind the steady temperatures, and the wind belt's path behind the rainfall.  Storage tanks, packing badly for a winter, and following the averages are all things that FOLLOW from those causes, which is what makes them consequences rather than explanations.

items.stem: A {{0}} is the record a station gets compared against, and a station's own record is the only one allowed.

choices: baseline
average
range

distractorRationale.1: An average is the years added together and divided by how many there were.  It describes what an ordinary year looks like;  it is not the reference record a station gets measured against.
