distractorRationale.2: A range is the distance between the highest reading and the lowest one, which is a spread inside a station's record rather than the record used as a reference.

items.quote: A baseline is the record a station gets compared against, and a station's own record is the only one allowed.
items.explain: The manual keeps its three words apart by what each one does: an average summarises, a range measures a spread, and a baseline is the reference a station gets compared against.  The second half of this sentence carries the rule that makes the word matter, since a station's own thirty-year history is the only record allowed to serve as that reference.

items.stem: A report explains Cairn Bay's forty-two inches of rain by pointing to the current along its coast.  What is wrong with that report?
choices: It has explained the rainfall column with the temperature column's cause.
It has the figure wrong;  Cairn Bay averages nine inches a year.
Nothing is wrong, since the current shapes the whole climate there.
It should have used a single year instead of the ten-year average.

distractorRationale.1: Nine inches is Sable Flats.  Cairn Bay averages forty-two, so the number in the report is right and only the cause attached to it is wrong.
distractorRationale.2: The manual rules that pairing out by name: the current does not explain the rainfall, and the wind's path does not explain the swing.
distractorRationale.3: A single year cannot overturn a decade, which is the reason the table averages ten of them.  Swapping to one year would make the report less reliable, not more.

items.explain: The manual pairs each column with its own cause: water and the current explain the temperature range, and the wind belt's path over ocean or land explains the rainfall.  A swapped report can land on the right number for entirely the wrong reason, which is worse than an obvious error because the next operative inherits it without noticing.

items.stem: Two posts report the same average summer high.  According to the manual, what can you still not conclude?
choices: That the two posts have kept records for the same number of years.
That both averages were worked out the same way.
That both posts file a ten-year table at all.
That their readings spread out by the same amount above and below it.

distractorRationale.0: How long a record runs is a separate matter from what its numbers say.  Sharing an average tells you nothing either way about record length.
distractorRationale.1: Every post's average is the years added and divided by how many there were;  that is simply the definition.  What can still differ is the spread hidden behind the same figure.
distractorRationale.2: The manual opens by saying every post on the network files one, so that much is never in doubt.

items.explain: An average and a range answer different questions, which is why the manual keeps them apart: two posts can share an average while sharing nothing else, and the range is usually where the real difference shows itself.  Sable Flats and Cairn Bay make the point at full size, swinging sixty-eight degrees against thirty-three.

items.stem: According to the transfer briefing, what should an operative's gear list follow?
choices: The weather on the day the transfer arrives.
The post's ten-year averages.
The wettest year the post has on record.
Whatever gear the previous operative left behind.

distractorRationale.0: The briefing warns against exactly that, since one week is weather rather than the year a kit has to cover.
distractorRationale.2: Packing for a single extreme year is the opposite of packing for the average, and the briefing points transfers at the averages.
distractorRationale.3: Nothing in the briefing mentions inherited kit.  It sends every transfer to the ten-year averages instead.

items.explain: The briefing closes on this rule because both posts punish the same mistake in opposite directions: a transfer landing at Sable Flats during a wet spell and one landing at Cairn Bay during a cold snap will each pack badly for the year that follows.  Packing for the average and carrying for the extreme is the whole advice.

items.stem: Match each of the manual's three words to what it actually tells an operative.
colLabels: The station's own thirty-year record, used as the reference
The distance between the highest reading and the lowest
What an ordinary year looks like at this post
items.explain: The three words do different jobs and the manual keeps them apart on purpose: an average summarises a typical year, a baseline is the reference a station gets compared against, and a range measures how far the extremes sit apart.  Mixing the average up with the baseline is the usual slip, since both are single figures that describe a whole record.

partA.stem: Why does the memo build a hatch-date column instead of working from the first-egg dates directly?
choices: A chick eats nothing before it hatches, so hatching is when the food has to be there.
The first-egg dates in the record are less accurate than the hatch dates.
The herring arrive on the same day the colony lays its first eggs.
The colony stopped moving its laying date earlier once the fledge rate fell.

partB.stem: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer you just gave?
choices: The thirtieth season's March tenth puts it around April first.
Tern eggs take about twenty-two days to hatch, and a chick eats nothing at all before it hatches.
The useful column is the hatch date, and the record lets us build that column ourselves.
The herring arrival has held near April twenty-first every season, and it has drifted only about three days either way.

distractorRationale.1: The memo never questions the first-egg dates.  It builds the hatch column out of them, so the hatch date is more useful rather than more accurate.
distractorRationale.2: The herring hold near April twenty-first every season no matter when the eggs are laid.  Their arrival is not tied to the colony's laying date at all.
distractorRationale.3: First eggs kept moving earlier right through the record, reaching March tenth by the thirtieth season, even while the fledge rate was falling.

items.explain: Eggs take about twenty-two days to hatch and a chick eats nothing before it hatches, so the date that decides whether food is available is the hatch date rather than the laying date.  Building that column from the record is what lets the memo set the chicks and the herring against each other honestly.

partA.stem: According to the memo, why have the terns and the herring shifted their timing at such different rates?
choices: The herring have not been tracked for as many seasons as the colony has.
Each reads a different cue, and the sea warms far more slowly than coastal air.
The terns have been failing to respond to their surroundings properly.
The mismatch began with the fish arriving later each season.

partB.stem: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer you just gave?
choices: These terns respond just as they are built to respond.
The mismatch did not start with the fish.
The herring read ocean temperature out at sea, and the sea warms slowly.
The herring arrival has held near April twenty-first every season, and it has drifted only about three days either way.

distractorRationale.0: The memo reports the herring arrival for every season alongside the colony's own dates.  Both run the length of the same record.
distractorRationale.2: The memo says the birds are not doing anything wrong and respond just as they are built to.  The cue changed underneath them; the response did not fail.
distractorRationale.3: The memo states plainly that the mismatch did not start with the fish, and the herring arrival has barely moved across thirty seasons.

items.explain: The terns time their nesting to coastal air, which has warmed quickly across thirty seasons, while the herring time their run to ocean temperature, and the sea warms slowly.  Two clocks reading two different cues will drift apart even when both animals behave exactly as they always have.

partA.stem: What does the memo mean when it calls this an adaptation limit?
choices: A species runs short of food once its own population grows too large.
A colony stops responding to its surroundings after enough bad seasons.
A species can follow its own cue and no further, even once that cue stops predicting the food.
A record stops being reliable once it has run for thirty seasons.

partB.stem: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer you just gave?
choices: These terns respond just as they are built to respond.
An animal can shift its timing only as far and as fast as its own cue shifts.
Their cue used to predict the food, and now it does not.
The useful column is the hatch date, and the record lets us build that column ourselves.

distractorRationale.0: The memo never mentions population size.  The limit it describes is about timing, where the cue that used to predict the food no longer does.
distractorRationale.1: The terns keep responding exactly as they are built to.  Nothing in the memo shows them stopping.
distractorRationale.3: The memo treats the thirty-season record as its most reliable tool, using it to build the hatch column.  Its length is a strength here rather than a flaw.

items.explain: An adaptation limit is a limit on how far a response can carry, not a failure of the response itself: the terns shift exactly as far as their own cue shifts, and no further.  Their cue used to predict the herring and no longer does, which is why responding correctly has stopped being enough.

partA.stem: The memo warns Command not to accept one good season as evidence of recovery.  What would count instead?
choices: A single season in which the chicks hatch after the herring have arrived.
The colony's first eggs moving back toward April seventh.
The herring beginning to arrive three weeks earlier than they now do.
Chick survival rising across several seasons in a row rather than in one strong year.

partB.stem: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer you just gave?
choices: It would look like the fledge column climbing across several seasons in a row.
One good season is weather rather than recovery, and Command should not be sold one.
The herring arrival has held near April twenty-first every season, and it has drifted only about three days either way.
First eggs came on April seventh in the first logged season, so the eggs hatched around April twenty-ninth.

distractorRationale.0: The memo says outright that one good season is weather rather than recovery.  A single season proves nothing in either direction.
distractorRationale.1: April seventh is where the record began, not a target to return to.  The memo measures recovery by chick survival rather than by the calendar date the colony nests on.
distractorRationale.2: Herring arriving three weeks earlier would genuinely close the timing gap, so the idea is not wrong about the science.  It is wrong about this record: the herring have drifted only about three days in thirty seasons, and the memo defines recovery by the fledge column instead.

items.explain: A single strong season is ordinary variation, the same way one warm year is weather rather than a trend, so the memo asks for the fledge column to climb across several seasons in a row before anyone calls it recovery.  That standard is about the number of seasons agreeing, not about how good the best one looks.

items.stem: Choose the three statements the memo's hatch-date column actually supports.
choices: The chicks in the first logged season hatched before the herring arrived.
The herring arrival has moved about as far as the colony's nesting date has.
Tern eggs take about twenty-two days to hatch.
By the thirtieth season the chicks were hatching about three weeks before the herring.
The fledge rate rose as the hatch date moved earlier.
By the tenth season the chicks were already hatching before the herring got there.

distractorRationale.0: In the first logged season the chicks hatched eight days AFTER the herring had already arrived.  That is the one season in the memo where the food was there first.
distractorRationale.1: The herring arrival has drifted only about three days either way across thirty seasons, while the colony's first eggs moved from April seventh to March tenth.
distractorRationale.4: The fledge column falls across the record, from seventy-six percent in the first season to thirty-nine percent by the thirtieth.

items.explain: The memo builds its hatch column from the pinned incubation of about twenty-two days, and that column places the chicks after the herring in the first logged season, before them by the tenth, and about three weeks before them by the thirtieth.  The herring have drifted about three days across those thirty seasons, which is a real shift and simply a far smaller one than the colony's.  Each wrong choice reverses one of those states or credits the herring with a shift on the colony's scale.

items.stem: Tap the two sentences that name the date the memo rules OUT and give the reason for ruling it out.
spans: The question worth Command's time is a different one.
Start with the date that matters, which is not the day the first eggs appear.
Tern eggs take about twenty-two days to hatch, and a chick eats nothing at all before it hatches.
The useful column is the hatch date, and the record lets us build that column ourselves.
Now set the herring beside that column.
items.explain: One sentence rules out the laying date and the next gives the reason, which is that eggs take about twenty-two days and a chick eats nothing before it hatches.  The other three announce that a question is coming, restate the conclusion once it has already been reached, or move on to the herring, so none of them carries the reasoning itself.

items.stem: Tap the two sentences that each name the cue one of the two animals actually reads.
spans: By the thirtieth season they were hatching about three weeks before.
Two clocks are running here, and they run at different speeds.
The terns read the coastal air, which has warmed quickly over thirty seasons.
The herring read ocean temperature out at sea, and the sea warms slowly.
The mismatch did not start with the fish.
items.explain: Each keyed sentence names one animal and the specific signal it responds to, along with how fast that signal has been moving.  The sentence about two clocks announces that the cues differ without saying what either one is, while the other two report the resulting gap and rule out the fish as its origin.

items.stem: An animal can shift its timing only as far and as fast as its own {{0}} shifts.

choices: food
season
cue

distractorRationale.0: The food is what the cue used to predict, not the thing the animal reads.  The memo's whole point is that the signal and the food have come apart.
distractorRationale.1: A season is when things happen rather than a signal an animal can respond to.  The memo names coastal air as what the terns actually read.

items.quote: An animal can shift its timing only as far and as fast as its own cue shifts.
items.explain: An adaptation limit is a limit on the signal, not on the animal: a tern can follow its own cue as far as that cue moves and no further, however badly it needs the food to be there.  That is why the memo insists the birds are not doing anything wrong, since their cue used to predict the herring and simply no longer does.

items.stem: The record's twentieth season shows first eggs on March eighteenth.  According to the memo, about when did those eggs hatch?
choices: Around the eighteenth of March, the same day.
Around the twenty-first of April, when the herring arrive.
Around the ninth of April.
Around the twenty-ninth of April.

distractorRationale.0: Tern eggs take about twenty-two days to hatch, so hatching cannot fall on the day the first egg appears.
distractorRationale.1: April twenty-first is the herring's date, not the colony's.  The memo's whole point is that the two dates no longer line up.
distractorRationale.3: April twenty-ninth is the FIRST season's hatch date, when first eggs came on April seventh.  By the twentieth season the eggs were coming nearly three weeks earlier.

items.explain: The memo builds its hatch column by adding the pinned incubation of about twenty-two days to each season's first-egg date, so March eighteenth puts hatching around April ninth.  That column is the one that matters, because a chick eats nothing before it hatches and the herring hold near April twenty-first whatever the colony does.

items.stem: Command asks whether one strong season would prove the colony is recovering.  How does the memo answer?
choices: No, because a single season is ordinary variation rather than a trend.
Yes, if the fledge rate climbs back above seventy-six percent.
Yes, provided the herring also arrive earlier that same year.
No, because thirty seasons is too short a record to show recovery.

distractorRationale.1: Seventy-six percent is the first season's figure, not a threshold the memo sets.  It asks for several seasons climbing in a row, whatever level they reach.
distractorRationale.2: The memo defines recovery by the fledge column across seasons, and the herring have drifted only about three days in thirty of them.
distractorRationale.3: The memo treats the thirty-season record as its most reliable tool.  What it wants is a run of good seasons, not a longer record.

items.explain: One good season is weather, in the same way one warm year is weather rather than a trend, so the memo asks for the fledge column to climb across several seasons in a row before anyone reports recovery to Command.  The standard is about how many seasons agree with each other, not about how good the best one looks.

items.stem: A different seabird times its nesting to day length, which does not change from year to year.  Following the memo's reasoning, what would warming do to that bird's nesting date?
choices: Move it earlier, since every bird responds to a warmer spring.
Stop it nesting altogether once its food moved.
Make its eggs take longer than twenty-two days to hatch.
Leave it steady, because the cue it reads has not moved.

distractorRationale.0: The memo's point is that a bird follows its OWN cue.  A bird reading day length has no warming signal to respond to at all.
distractorRationale.1: Nothing in the memo describes a colony ceasing to nest.  The terns kept nesting throughout, which is exactly what made the mismatch visible in the fledge column.
distractorRationale.2: Incubation length is not the cue, and the memo never links it to warming.  What shifts, or fails to shift, is the date nesting begins.

items.explain: An animal can shift its timing only as far and as fast as its own cue shifts, so a bird cued by day length would hold its date however warm the spring became.  That is the same reasoning the memo uses on the terns from the other side: they moved twenty-eight days because their cue moved, not because they chose to.

items.stem: In six words or fewer, name the signal the terns read when they decide it is time to nest.
accept: the temperature of the coastal air
items.explain: The memo names the two cues side by side: the terns read the coastal air, which has warmed quickly across thirty seasons, while the herring read ocean temperature out at sea, and the sea warms slowly.  Naming the tern cue is what makes the whole mismatch legible, since the birds are responding correctly to a signal that no longer predicts their food.

partA.stem: Why does the board rule that Proposal D's petition half still cannot count, when the other half clears every gate?
choices: Joining two plans collects their weaknesses instead of averaging them out.
The feeding station stops working once a petition is filed alongside it.
The board is not permitted to consider any option beyond the three filed.
Proposal D would cost more than this year's field budget allows.

partB.stem: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer you just gave?
choices: Whatever the feeding station does on its own it still does, and whatever it does not do it still does not do.
The petition half still asks for an outcome outside the Network's own authority, and it still cannot be decided inside the one-season window.
The second member raised a fourth option, entered in the minutes as Proposal D.
Bolting two plans together does not average their weaknesses out.

distractorRationale.1: The board says the opposite: whatever the feeding station does on its own it still does.  Pairing it with the petition changes neither half.
distractorRationale.2: The board did consider it, entering it in the minutes as Proposal D.  It failed on its merits rather than being ruled out for arriving late.
distractorRationale.3: The board names two problems with the petition half, authority and the one-season window.  Cost is not among them.

items.explain: A combined plan has to clear every constraint that either half has to clear, so the petition's two failures, authority and the one-season window, travel into Proposal D unchanged.  Pairing a failing part with a working part does not average the two; the board records that it collects them.

partA.stem: What does the chair mean by calling Command's three constraints gates rather than scores?
choices: Each constraint is worth points, and the highest total across the three wins.
Failing any one of them puts a proposal out, however well it does on the others.
The board scores the proposals and sends its own ranking to Command.
A constraint can be lowered if none of the proposals manages to clear it.

partB.stem: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer you just gave?
choices: Only the proposals clearing all three get compared against each other, and only then does anybody discuss which one is better.
The window is a constraint Command set, and Command is the only body that can change it.
A proposal failing one gate is out of the running, however strong it happens to look on the other two.
The board does not choose.

distractorRationale.0: The board compares proposals only after all three constraints are cleared, so a comparison never runs across a failed one.  Points would let a strong showing cover a failure.
distractorRationale.2: The minutes say the board does not choose.  It records how the choosing has to be done and leaves the recommendation with the operative.
distractorRationale.3: Only Command can change a constraint Command set, and the board specifically declined to widen the window itself.

items.explain: A gate is pass or fail: clearing two constraints beautifully earns nothing if the third fails, because the proposal never reaches the comparison stage at all.  Scores would let a strong showing on cost or speed quietly cover a failure on authority, which is exactly what the chair wanted ruled out in writing.

partA.stem: The fourth member asks the board to widen the one-season window.  Why does the board decline?
choices: Two seasons still would not be long enough for the petition to be decided.
The request was ruled out of order and struck from the minutes.
Changing a constraint is not the same as meeting it, and only Command can change this one.
The board had already settled on a proposal before the request was raised.

partB.stem: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer you just gave?
choices: The board does not choose.
Asking for an easier constraint is not the same thing as meeting the one in front of you.
The request was recorded and forwarded to Command as a separate item, and the evaluation continues under the window as written.
The petition half still asks for an outcome outside the Network's own authority, and it still cannot be decided inside the one-season window.

distractorRationale.0: Widening the window would clear the petition's TIMING problem, so time is not the objection here.  The board declined because the window is Command's to change rather than the board's, and the authority gate would still stand however wide the window got.
distractorRationale.1: The request was recorded and forwarded to Command as its own item.  Declining to act on a request is not the same as striking it.
distractorRationale.3: The board does not choose at all.  Its job is to record how the choosing has to be done.

items.explain: The board separates two different moves: meeting the constraint in front of you, and asking for a different constraint.  Only Command can change a window Command set, so the request goes forward as its own item while the evaluation continues under the window as written.

items.stem: Choose the three findings the review board actually recorded in its minutes.
choices: A plan built from two parts carries the weaknesses of both parts.
Only proposals clearing all three constraints get compared with each other.
The one response aimed at the fish rather than the colony lies outside the Network's authority.
The board ranked the three filed proposals from strongest to weakest.
The board widened the review window to two seasons.
The petition may be counted toward this season's approved response.

distractorRationale.3: The minutes say the board does not choose.  It records the method and leaves the recommendation with the operative.
distractorRationale.4: The board declined to widen the window, since only Command can change a constraint Command set.  The request was forwarded rather than granted.
distractorRationale.5: The board records the opposite: the petition cannot count toward this season's approved response, because its outcome lies outside the Network's authority.

items.explain: The three findings are the method the chair asked to have entered word for word, the ruling that a combined plan collects its parts' weaknesses, and the closing line about where each response is AIMED.  The petition is the one thing on the table aimed at the fish rather than at the colony, and it is also the one thing the Network cannot decide for itself.  Each wrong choice credits the board with an action it explicitly refused: ranking the proposals, widening a constraint, or letting the petition count toward this season.

partA.stem: Command's warning procedure leans toward calling a front early on purpose.  Which trade-off does that choice accept?
choices: Officers have to track more than four readings every morning.
Warnings will tend to arrive at the same time as the rain does.
The colony count has to be folded into the warning decision.
Some harbors get emptied for nothing, so that no warning ever arrives too late.

partB.stem: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer you just gave?
choices: The colony line belongs at the bottom of the page and stays out of the warning decision entirely.
At least two of the four tracked readings must move together, from one morning to the next.
A warning arriving alongside the rain is not a warning at all.
A warning nobody needed empties a harbor for a single day, while a warning that came late costs boats and the crews aboard them.

distractorRationale.0: The procedure works from the same four readings throughout.  Leaning early changes when a call gets made, not how many instruments an officer reads.
distractorRationale.1: That is the outcome leaning early exists to avoid.  A warning arriving with the rain is not a warning at all, only a report.
distractorRationale.2: The colony line stays out of the warning decision entirely, whichever way the procedure leans.

items.explain: Two mistakes are possible and they do not cost the same: an unnecessary warning empties a harbor for a day, while a late warning costs boats and crews.  Command accepts the cheaper mistake more often in order to make the expensive one rare, which is a design choice about which failure to tolerate.

items.stem: Tap the two sentences that state what happens to a proposal that fails a single one of Command's constraints.
spans: The chair opened with the method and asked that it go into the minutes word for word.
Command's three constraints are gates rather than scores, and a proposal either clears a gate or it does not.
A proposal failing one gate is out of the running, however strong it happens to look on the other two.
Only the proposals clearing all three get compared against each other, and only then does anybody discuss which one is better.
The second member raised a fourth option, entered in the minutes as Proposal D.
items.explain: The keyed pair carries the pass-or-fail rule: a proposal either clears a gate or it does not, and failing one puts it out however strong it looks on the other two.  The comparison sentence describes what happens to proposals that PASS all three, and the other two record who was speaking rather than what the rule is.

items.stem: Tap the three sentences that state why joining two plans does not repair the weaker one.
spans: Bolting two plans together does not average their weaknesses out.
It collects them.
The petition half still asks for an outcome outside the Network's own authority, and it still cannot be decided inside the one-season window.
Neither problem gets any smaller by pairing the petition with something that works.
The board therefore records that the petition cannot count toward this season's approved response.
items.explain: The three keyed sentences give the general principle and then apply it: weaknesses are collected rather than averaged, so pairing the petition with something that works leaves both of its problems exactly the size they were.  The other two name the petition's specific failures and record the ruling that follows, which are the inputs and the output of the reasoning rather than the reasoning itself.

items.stem: The window is a {{0}} Command set, and Command is the only body that can change it.

choices: constraint
proposal
finding

distractorRationale.1: A proposal is one of the responses being evaluated.  The window is the thing proposals get measured against, which is the opposite side of the evaluation.
distractorRationale.2: A finding is what the board records after it evaluates something.  The window existed before the board ever met, because Command set it.

items.quote: The window is a constraint Command set, and Command is the only body that can change it.
items.explain: A constraint is a limit the evaluation runs under rather than anything produced by the evaluation, which is exactly why the board could forward the request to widen the window but could not grant it.  Proposals are what gets judged and findings are what the judging produces, so neither one can be the thing that sets the terms.

items.stem: What does the review board actually record about Proposal D?
choices: That Proposal D replaces Proposal A as the recommended plan.
That its petition half cannot count toward this season's approved response.
That Proposal D clears all three constraints once the halves are combined.
That Proposal D is out of order for being raised after the filing.

distractorRationale.0: The board does not choose at all.  It records how the choosing has to be done and leaves the recommendation with the operative.
distractorRationale.2: Combining collects the weaknesses rather than averaging them away, so the petition's two failures travel into Proposal D unchanged.
distractorRationale.3: It was entered in the minutes as Proposal D and evaluated on its merits.  Nothing was dismissed for arriving late.

items.explain: The board finds that bolting two plans together does not average their weaknesses out but collects them, so the petition half still asks for an outcome outside the Network's authority and still cannot be decided inside the one-season window.  Its ruling is narrow and specific: the petition cannot be counted toward this season's approved response.

items.stem: A fifth proposal is cheap, fast and fully within the Network's authority.  A sixth is cheaper still but lies outside that authority.  How does the board's method treat them?
choices: The sixth wins, since cost is the constraint Command names first.
Both go forward, with the lower cost breaking the tie between them.
The fifth joins the comparison;  the sixth is out whatever it costs.
Neither goes forward until Command agrees to widen a constraint.

distractorRationale.0: Command's first constraint is a real effect on chick survival within one nesting season, not cost, and in any case no constraint outranks another when all three are gates.
distractorRationale.1: A proposal failing the authority gate never reaches the comparison stage at all, so there is no tie for cost to break.
distractorRationale.3: The fifth clears all three constraints exactly as written.  Asking for an easier constraint is not the same thing as meeting the one in front of you.

items.explain: Constraints are gates rather than scores, so clearing two of them beautifully earns nothing if the third fails: the proposal never reaches the stage where anybody discusses which option is better.  Being cheapest is a trade-off, and trade-offs only start to matter among the proposals that have already cleared every gate.

items.stem: According to the minutes, what is the review board's own job?
choices: To rank the proposals and forward that ranking to Command.
To change any constraint that none of the proposals can clear.
To file the operative's recommendation on the operative's behalf.
To record how the choosing has to be done, rather than to choose.

distractorRationale.0: The minutes say the board does not choose.  Ranking is precisely what it declined to do.
distractorRationale.1: Only Command can change a constraint Command set, which is why the board forwarded the request to widen the window rather than granting it.
distractorRationale.2: The recommendation stays with the operative.  The board's minutes record the method before that filing happens.

items.explain: The minutes open and close on the same point: the board does not choose, it records how the choosing has to be done.  That is why the chair asked for the gates-not-scores method to go into the record word for word, and why a request to widen a constraint was forwarded to Command as a separate item rather than acted on.

items.stem: In five words or fewer, name what the chair says Command's three constraints act as.
items.explain: The chair asks for one word to go into the minutes word for word: the three constraints are gates rather than scores.  A gate is passed or failed, so a proposal failing any one of them is out however strong it looks on the other two, and only the proposals clearing all three are ever compared against each other.

items.stem: Watch the moving trace on the plate. Which way does the signal travel, and why does that direction fit what the plate maps?
items.explain: The plate's own printed caption names these as the skin's nerves, and skin nerves carry feeling from the body back to the spine. The trace runs that way. If it ran outward, it would be teaching the opposite of what the picture is a map of.
choices: Away from the spine, because the brain sends every signal outward to the skin.
Toward the spine, because the plate maps the nerves that move the arm.
Both ways at once, because the front and back plates run in opposite directions.
Toward the spine, because the plate maps the skin's nerves, which carry feeling inward.

distractorRationale.0: This describes a command travelling out to a muscle. The plate maps the SKIN's nerves, and the trace runs the other way, toward the spine.
distractorRationale.1: The direction is right, but the reason is not. The plate's own printed caption names these as the skin's nerves, not the ones that move a limb.
distractorRationale.2: The two tabs are two views of the same body, front and back. Only one trace runs, and it runs one way.

items.stem: Choose the three statements that the plate itself actually shows.
choices: There are two views on tabs, one of the front and one of the back.
Each view is a whole standing figure, not a close-up of one limb.
A trace runs along the arm and travels toward the spine.
The plate labels each muscle the arm uses to lift a load.
A cutaway shows the brain and the spinal cord inside the body.

distractorRationale.3: No muscle is labelled anywhere on either view. The plate maps nerve territories in the skin.
distractorRationale.4: Neither view opens the body up. Both are outside views of a whole standing figure.

items.explain: Three things are on the plate and two are not. Two tabs give a front and a back view, each of a whole standing figure, and a trace runs along the arm toward the spine. No muscles are labelled and nothing is cut away to show the brain or spinal cord.

items.stem: On the life-support diagram, which box is labelled as a component?
items.explain: The diagram puts its labels right on the boxes. The bottom row holds the scrubber cartridge, the filter membrane and the light panel, and each carries the label component. Air, Water and Food are one row up, labelled subsystem, and Life Support at the top is the system.
choices: Scrubber cartridge
Air
Life Support
Water

distractorRationale.2: Life Support is the top box, and the diagram labels it the system. It is the largest level shown, not the smallest.
distractorRationale.3: Water is on the same row as Air and Food, and the diagram labels all three subsystems.

items.stem: The diagram nests its boxes one way only. Put these three levels in order from the smallest thing shown to the largest.
tiles: Air, a subsystem
Filter membrane, a component
Life Support, the system

items.stem: Across the days the chart covers, what happens to the two lines?
items.explain: The chart has two panels. The top one takes carbon dioxide from 410 to 430 to 452 parts per million, climbing the whole way. The bottom one takes oxygen from 20.5 to 20.0 to 19.5 percent, falling the whole way. One goes up, one goes down, and neither turns around.
choices: Both lines climb, one faster than the other.
Carbon dioxide climbs the whole way while oxygen falls the whole way.
Carbon dioxide climbs at first and then levels off near the end.
Oxygen falls at first and then recovers by the last day.

distractorRationale.0: Only one climbs. The oxygen panel starts at 20.5 percent and ends at 19.5, so that line falls.
distractorRationale.2: It does not level off. The three points read 410, then 430, then 452, so the rise from the middle to the end is the larger one.
distractorRationale.3: There is no recovery. Oxygen reads 20.5, then 20.0, then 19.5, falling by the same half point each time.

items.stem: Read the two panels. Carbon dioxide starts at {{0}} parts per million and ends at {{1}}, while oxygen ends at {{2}} percent.

distractorRationale.1: 430 is the middle reading, taken on the day between the first and the last, not the starting one.
distractorRationale.2: 452 is where carbon dioxide ends up, not where it begins.

distractorRationale.0: 410 is the first reading on the chart, not the last.
distractorRationale.1: 430 is the middle reading. The line keeps climbing past it.
20.0 is the middle oxygen reading, not the final one.
distractorRationale.2: 20.5 is where oxygen starts. It falls from there.

items.explain: Both panels give three readings each. Carbon dioxide runs 410, 430, 452 parts per million, so it starts at 410 and ends at 452. Oxygen runs 20.5, 20.0, 19.5 percent, so it ends at 19.5.

items.stem: The two panels are drawn on two separate scales. Why does that matter when you read them?
items.explain: One panel counts parts per million and the other counts percent, so the same amount of ink means different things in each. That makes a comparison inside one panel fair, and a comparison of steepness across the two meaningless. The caption says so too.
choices: Because it means one panel's readings are more accurate than the other's.
Because the two quantities are actually measured in the same unit underneath.
Because a line's steepness can only be compared inside its own panel, not across the two.
Because it means the two lines must cross somewhere between the days shown.

distractorRationale.0: Separate scales say nothing about accuracy. Both panels report real readings; they just measure different quantities in different units.
distractorRationale.1: They are not. One panel is parts per million and the other is a percent, which is exactly why they cannot share a scale.
distractorRationale.3: Lines on separate scales cannot be expected to cross at all. Where each sits on the page depends on its own panel's scale.

items.stem: The diagram puts each box on a row and labels that row. Match each box to the level the diagram gives it.
items.explain: This diagram uses position to mean something. Life Support sits alone at the top and is labelled the system. Air sits on the middle row with Water and Food, all labelled subsystems. The scrubber cartridge sits on the bottom row, labelled a component, with nothing drawn beneath it.

items.stem: In the cross-section, what happens to the warm air where the front is drawn?
items.explain: The cross-section shows cold air sliding in low and shoving the warm air up above it. Air that rises cools, its moisture condenses into cloud, and the rain falls from there. That is the whole chain the picture draws.
choices: It slides in low, underneath the cold air.
It is held in place by the cold air and stops moving.
It sinks and dries out as the cold air passes over the top of it.
It is forced upward, and its moisture condenses into clouds that drop rain.

distractorRationale.0: That is what the cold air does. The diagram draws the cold air wedging in below and the warm air going up.
distractorRationale.1: Nothing in the diagram is still. The warm air is pushed up, which is what makes the clouds.
distractorRationale.2: The diagram has the cold air below, not above, and the warm air rising rather than sinking.

items.stem: In the diagram, the cold air slides in {{0}} the warm air, and the moisture in the rising warm air condenses into {{1}}.

choices: beneath
above
away from

distractorRationale.2: The two do not separate. The whole picture is about what happens where they meet.

choices: clouds
a wind shift
falling pressure

distractorRationale.2: Falling pressure is another of the listed warning signs, and it is a reading, not something moisture becomes.

items.explain: The diagram is a side view of the two air masses meeting. Cold air comes in beneath, the warm air is forced up, and the moisture it carries condenses into clouds. The wind shift and falling pressure sit in the note as early signs, not as what the moisture becomes.

items.stem: On the surface map, one line carries filled triangles along it. Which kind of front is that?
items.explain: The map draws its fronts with symbols rather than words. Triangles alone mark a cold front, semicircles alone mark a warm front, and a line carrying both alternating on opposite sides marks a stationary front.
choices: A cold front
A warm front
A stationary front
An isobar

distractorRationale.1: A warm front is drawn with filled semicircles, not triangles.
distractorRationale.2: A stationary front carries both symbols, triangles and semicircles alternating on opposite sides of the line.
distractorRationale.3: An isobar is not a front at all. On this map isobars are plain lines labelled with pressure values from 993 to 1016.

items.stem: Choose the three things this surface map actually puts on the page.
choices: Fronts drawn as lines carrying triangles or semicircles.
Pressure centres marked with the letters H and L.
Isobars labelled with pressure values between 993 and 1016.
A forecast of what the weather will do over the next three days.
A photograph of the storm taken from a satellite.

distractorRationale.4: There is no photograph on this map. It is a drawn chart of symbols, letters and labelled lines.

items.stem: Read the rainfall panel. Which post gets more rain in an average year, and roughly how much more?
items.explain: The rainfall panel gives one bar per post: Sable Flats at 9 inches a year, Cairn Bay at 42. Dividing 42 by 9 gives a little under five, so Cairn Bay gets close to five times the rain. The 68 and 33 belong to the other panel and are degrees of seasonal swing.
choices: Cairn Bay, at 42 inches against Sable Flats' 9, so getting about twice as much.
Cairn Bay, at 42 inches against Sable Flats' 9, so getting close to five times as much.
Sable Flats, at 68 inches against Cairn Bay's 33.
Neither, because the two bars in the rainfall panel are the same height.

distractorRationale.2: Those are the two seasonal swings, read off the other panel, and they are degrees rather than inches.
distractorRationale.3: They are far apart. The rainfall panel puts Sable Flats at 9 inches and Cairn Bay at 42.

distractorRationale.2: 96 degrees is Sable Flats' summer high from the notes, not the size of its swing.

distractorRationale.2: 41 degrees is Cairn Bay's winter low from the notes, not its swing.

A driest year on record of 5 inches

One sits at a much higher elevation than the other.
One sits on the coast with a current nearby, and the other sits well inland in dry continental air.
The wind belt blows off the ocean and reaches both posts equally wet.

items.stem: Read the fledge-rate line across the thirty seasons. What does it do?
items.explain: The line gives four readings: 76 percent at season 1, then 64, then 52, then 39. Every step is lower than the one before, and the last is about half the first rather than close to nothing.

It holds steady until about season 20, then drops sharply.
It drops almost to zero by season 30.
It falls at every step, from 76 percent down to 39.

distractorRationale.2: It ends at 39 percent, which is a serious fall but nowhere near zero. The axis runs to 100, so the height is easy to read honestly.

items.stem: The fledge rate starts at {{0}} percent in season 1 and ends at {{1}} percent in season 30, which is roughly {{2}} of where it began.

distractorRationale.0: 64 percent is the season 10 reading, one step in.
distractorRationale.2: 52 percent is the season 20 reading, two steps in.

distractorRationale.1: 52 percent is the season 20 reading. The line keeps falling after it.
distractorRationale.2: 30 is the last season number on the bottom axis, not a fledge rate.

choices: half
a fifth
a tenth

distractorRationale.1: A fifth is what the fall looks like if the axis is read as though it started at 30 rather than 0. Against the real 0 to 100 axis, 39 is about half of 76.
distractorRationale.2: A tenth of 76 would be under 8 percent. The line ends at 39.

items.explain: The line runs 76, 64, 52, 39. Dividing 39 by 76 gives just over one half, so the colony's fledge rate ends at roughly half of where it started. The axis runs from 0 to 100, so the shape on the page matches that arithmetic instead of exaggerating it.

items.stem: Choose the three things this chart and its notes actually tell you.
choices: The fledge rate is lower at every reading than at the one before.
In season 1 the chicks hatched about eight days after the herring arrived.
By season 30 the chicks hatched about three weeks before the herring arrived.
The herring now arrive about a month later than they used to.
The colony will die out within the next ten seasons.

distractorRationale.3: The notes say the opposite about the herring: their arrival holds near April 21 every season, drifting only about three days either way. It is the chicks whose timing moved.
distractorRationale.4: The chart stops at season 30 and predicts nothing. A falling line is not a forecast of when it reaches zero.

items.explain: Three of these are on the chart or in its notes: the fall at every step, the eight days after in season 1, and the three weeks before by season 30. The herring did not move, which is the whole point, and nothing here forecasts an end date.

items.stem: The diagram is titled so that one station cannot see the pattern alone. Which detail on it explains why?
items.explain: The diagram separates two behaviours. Temperature climbs overall but bounces year to year, so a short local record can show a fall that is not the pattern. Carbon dioxide and fuel-use climb together and never reverse. Putting three stations side by side is what makes the bouncing average out.
choices: Temperature climbs overall while still bouncing year to year, so a single station's run of years can point either way.
Only Network Command records temperature, and the stations record nothing.
The three stations are too far apart to compare with one another.
Carbon dioxide reverses direction often, so no station can trust its own readings.

distractorRationale.1: The diagram says every station logs temperature and carbon dioxide. Command adds a fuel-use index on top of that.
distractorRationale.2: Distance is never given on the diagram, and the whole point is that their records are compared.
distractorRationale.3: The diagram says carbon dioxide and fuel-use climb on almost the same line and never reverse. It is temperature that bounces.

items.stem: Read down the three cards. Which proposal carries a YES on all three tests?
items.explain: Only Proposal A carries YES on all three tests: within budget, within authority, and a real effect while it runs. That is not the same as being the best plan, and the card says so itself: the effect ends when the station stops. B is aimed at the wrong cause, and C is the right fix with the wrong timeline and reach.
choices: Proposal C, the petition to delay the herring season
Proposal A, the feeding station
Proposal B, the fencing
None of them, because every card carries at least one NO

distractorRationale.0: C carries two NOs: it takes over four months, which runs past one season, and it sits outside the Network’s own authority. Its own card calls it the right fix with the wrong timeline and reach.
distractorRationale.2: B carries a NO of its own: the chicks are starving rather than being taken by predators, so fencing is fast and cheap but aimed at the wrong cause.
distractorRationale.3: One card has no NO on it. Proposal A is YES on budget, YES on authority and YES on effect while it runs.

items.stem: Choose the three statements that describe how this comparison panel is built.
choices: Every proposal is checked against the same three tests.
One of the three tests is whether the plan has an effect within one season.
Card B shows no verdict at all for the authority test.
Each proposal is checked against whichever tests suit it best.
Every card carries a YES on at least two of the three tests.

distractorRationale.3: That would defeat the point of a comparison panel. The header names three tests and every card is read down the same three.
distractorRationale.4: Card C carries only one YES, against two NOs, so this is not true of every card.

items.explain: The header names the three tests and every card is read down the same three, one of which is whether the plan has an effect within one season. Card B simply has no authority verdict on it, which the panel leaves empty rather than inventing. And card C carries only one YES, so no rule about "at least two" holds across all three.

items.stem: The panel's header lists the three tests in a fixed order. Put them in the order the header gives.
tiles: Cost within budget
Effect within one season
The Network's own authority
items.explain: The header reads: effect within one season, cost within budget, the Network's own authority. Every card is then read down that same order, which is what lets three proposals be compared at all.

items.stem: The proposals panel tests each plan for an effect within one season. The fledge-rate chart shows a decline measured across thirty seasons. What does putting those two together tell you about Proposal A, the feeding station?
items.explain: Read the two together and the mismatch is in the timescales. The panel measures each proposal by what it does within one season, and records that A's effect ends when the station stops. The chart measures a fall across thirty seasons. A can help while it runs and still leave the long decline untouched.
choices: It solves the decline, because the chart's fall is only about half and a feeding station covers that.
It fails the budget test, which is why the chart keeps falling.
It can help while it runs, but a one-season effect does not answer a thirty-season decline.
The two cannot be compared, because one is a chart and the other is a panel.

distractorRationale.0: The panel itself records that A's effect ends when the station stops. Something that stops is not a match for a trend measured across thirty seasons.
distractorRationale.1: The panel puts A within budget. The chart's fall has nothing to do with what a proposal costs.
distractorRationale.3: They are measured in the same unit that matters here, time. One tests an effect over a season; the other measures a change over thirty.

figures.caption: The field manual's own example: life support as one system, split into three subsystems, each built from its own components.
figures.credit: Outpost Network field manual (this pack's own diagram)
figures.alt: A tree diagram. At the top, a box labeled Life Support (system). Below it, three boxes labeled Air, Water, and Food (subsystem). Below each subsystem sits one component box: Scrubber cartridge under Air, Filter membrane under Water, Light panel under Food. Two notes below explain interaction: a clogged scrubber cartridge lets carbon dioxide climb, so the crew works slower and sleeps worse; dim light panels slow crop growth, so the crew eats more of what gets shipped in.

items: A tree diagram titled "Life support: system, subsystem, component".
The top box is Life Support, labelled (system).
Three boxes below it are Air, Water and Food, each labelled (subsystem).
Below those sit Scrubber cartridge, Filter membrane and Light panel, each labelled (component).
The nesting runs one way only: components sit inside subsystems, which sit inside the system.

figures.caption: A cold front in cross section: cold air slides in low and shoves warmer air up, where it cools and its moisture falls back down as rain.
figures.credit: Outpost Network field manual (this pack's own diagram)
figures.alt: A cross section along the ground. On the left, a wedge of cold air slides forward along the ground, labeled cold air slides in low. Where it meets the warm air, a green line marks the front. To the right, an arrow labeled warm air forced upward curves up into a cluster of clouds labeled moisture condenses into clouds, with rain falling from the clouds. A note below explains that falling pressure, rising humidity, a wind shift, then falling temperature and rising wind speed can flag a front a full day early.

items: A cross-section titled "Cold air meets warm air: how a front forms".
A boundary line is labelled front.
Cold air slides in low, beneath the warm air.
Warm air is forced upward above the cold air.
Moisture condenses into clouds where the warm air rises, and rain falls from them.
A note reads that falling pressure, rising humidity, a wind shift, then falling temperature and rising wind speed can flag a front a full day early.

figures.caption: Sable Flats and Cairn Bay share almost the same latitude, but a coast, an ocean current, and a wind belt that dries out over land give them very different climates.
figures.credit: Outpost Network field report (this pack's own map)
figures.alt: A map showing two posts at the same latitude, marked by a dashed line. On the left, Cairn Bay sits on the coast next to open ocean, with a current arrow along its coastline. On the right, Sable Flats sits well inland, over dry, continental land. A wide arrow labeled wind belt: blows off the ocean tapers as it crosses the land, labeled arrives far drier, drops its moisture along the way. Two boxes below summarize: Cairn Bay's coast and nearby current give it a smaller seasonal swing; Sable Flats' inland position with no current gives it a wider seasonal swing.

items: A comparison titled "Same latitude, different climate".
Both posts sit at the same latitude and receive the same sun angle all year.
Cairn Bay is on the coast, with an ocean current nearby.
Sable Flats is well inland, in dry continental air.
A wind belt blows off the ocean and arrives far drier inland, having dropped its moisture along the way.
Cairn Bay, on the coast with a current nearby, has the smaller seasonal swing.

figures.caption: Three proposals for Halyard Point, checked against Command's three tests: an effect within one season, cost within budget, and only the Network's own authority.
figures.credit: Outpost Network field report (this pack's own diagram)
figures.alt: Three side-by-side cards. Proposal A, a feeding station, passes all three tests but ends when the station stops. Proposal B, fencing, is within budget and quick to build but does not fix starving chicks, since predators are not the cause. Proposal C, a petition to delay the herring season, would close the mismatch at its root but takes over four months, past the one-season window, and lies outside the Network's own authority.

items: A three-card comparison titled "Three proposals for Halyard Point".
The header states that every proposal is checked against three tests: effect within one season, cost within budget, and the Network’s own authority.
Proposal A, a feeding station, carries YES on all three: within budget, within authority, and a real effect while it runs. Its card adds that the effect ends when the station stops.
Proposal B, fencing, carries YES within budget and YES ready in days, and a NO reading "starving chicks, not predators". Its card sums it up as fast and cheap, wrong cause.

Proposal C, a petition to delay the herring season, carries YES it closes the mismatch at its root, NO it takes over four months and so runs past one season, and NO it is outside the Network’s own authority. Its card sums it up as the right fix, wrong timeline and reach.
Card B shows no verdict for the authority test at all.
